edits.text:
Merger review: CCI combination order (feedback #6)

- Local file: `sources/CCI_Combination_C-2023-04-1022_AirIndia_Vistara.pdf`
  - Source: Competition Commission of India, Combination Registration No.
    C-2023/04/1022, order under Section 31(1), 1 September 2023 (Tata Sons, SIA,
    Air India, Talace, Tata SIA Airlines):
    <https://www.cci.gov.in/images/caseorders/en/order1695297548.pdf>
  - SHA-256: `172642fe416abe8a882ed498d25c42d5ae78300fabd1de3505547a86435cdc29`
  - Scanned PDF (no text layer), 73 pages: order pp. 1-45, then Annexures A-C
    (commitments). Page numbers below are the order's printed numbers.
  - p. 5 (para 12): Vistara merges into Air India; SIA ends with 25.1% of the
    merged entity (useful for MHHI, feedback #1).
  - p. 7 (para 19): relevant market is the origin-destination (O&D) city pair,
    not the national market. Air India and Vistara overlap on 48 domestic O&D pairs
    (Table 1, pp. 7-8).
  - p. 38 (paras 109-111): combined share above 40% on some overlapping routes in
    FY2022-23; CCI relies on rivals' slots and LCC competition for contestability.
  - p. 44 (paras 126-127): show-cause notice issued 27 June 2023; approved subject
    to voluntary commitments, "not likely to have any appreciable adverse effect
    on competition in India".
  - pp. 40-41 (paras 115-118): domestic commitment to keep minimum capacity on 7
    routes (DEL-COK, DEL-TRV, BLR-GAU, BBI-DEL, ATQ-DEL, BBI-BOM, BLR-DEL) for up
    to 4 years; share triggers are redacted.

% Sections 1 to 6 must fit in 2--3 pages. Appendices are not counted.

How did airline exits, acquisitions and mergers change ownership-adjusted concentration in India's scheduled domestic passenger market between January 2015 and July 2026, and do the resulting \HHI{}, \CRtwo{}, share-gap and fringe-share measures meet pre-defined thresholds for an asymmetric IndiGo--Air India Group duopoly?
\textbf{O1.} Track monthly market structure using brand-level \HHI{}, ownership-adjusted \HHI{}, modified \HHI{} (\MHHI{}), \CRtwo{} and the effective number of firms.\\
\textbf{O2.} Measure which airline groups absorbed the passengers and capacity of Jet Airways and Go First, and document the slot and fleet mechanisms.\\
\textbf{O3.} Assess whether airlines entering after 2015 became persistent competitors.\\
\textbf{O4.} Test whether the market meets explicit duopoly thresholds, and whether counting brands separately understates concentration.
\placeholder{One sentence: what changed after Assignment 1 feedback (three concentration series, explicit duopoly thresholds, claims restricted to market structure). See Appendix C.}

The main unit of analysis is the \textbf{market-month}: the Indian scheduled domestic passenger market in a given month, for which concentration measures are computed. These are built from a supporting unit, the \textbf{airline-month}, which records each airline's passengers and seat capacity. Airlines are aggregated into \textbf{ownership groups} for the ownership-adjusted measures (Air India and Air India Express throughout; Jet Airways and JetLite throughout; Vistara, AirAsia India and AIX Connect join the Air India Group from January 2022).

\textbf{Time period:} January 2015 to July 2026, monthly (138 market-months; April 2020 has no scheduled passenger traffic). \textbf{Geography:} all of India, at national level. \textbf{Market:} scheduled domestic passenger services only; international, charter and cargo-only operations are excluded. Route-level competition is outside the scope because the data does not record city pairs \placeholder{update if DGCA city-pair data is found, feedback \#3}.

response.value:
An **entry barrier** is anything that makes it hard for a new firm to start competing in a market.

**Example:** opening a tea stall needs a stove, a kettle and a corner of the street, so almost anyone can do it and entry barriers are low. Starting an airline needs aircraft costing hundreds of crores, airport landing slots, a DGCA licence, trained pilots and years of losses before profit. Very few can do that, so entry barriers are high.

**Common types**

| Type | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **High start-up cost** | You need a lot of money just to begin | Buying or leasing aircraft |
| **Government permission** | You need a licence or approval | DGCA operating permit, telecom spectrum |
| **Scarce resources** | The key input is limited and already taken | Airport slots at Delhi and Mumbai |
| **Economies of scale** | Big firms have lower cost per unit, so small newcomers can't match their prices | IndiGo's large fleet lowers its cost per seat |
| **Brand and loyalty** | Customers stick with known names | Frequent-flyer programmes |
| **Network effects** | The product is worth more when more people use it | WhatsApp, or an airline with more routes and connections |

**Why it matters**
- **Low barriers:** if firms make big profits, newcomers rush in, prices fall and profits shrink. That is why the table you shared shows zero long-run profit for perfect and monopolistic competition.
- **High barriers:** newcomers can't get in, so existing firms can keep high profits for a long time. That is why oligopoly and monopoly show "can persist."

**In your paper:** when Jet Airways and Go First exited, their slots and planes didn't go to new airlines. They went mostly to airlines that already had the scale, aircraft and slot access, especially IndiGo. That is entry barriers at work, and it is what your O2 analysis measures.

response.value:
This slide uses the **Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI)** to compare how concentrated different Indian markets are.

**How HHI works**
Square each firm's market share (in %) and add them up.
- Two firms with 50% each: $50^2 + 50^2 = 5{,}000$
- One firm with 100%: $100^2 = 10{,}000$ (pure monopoly)
- 100 firms with 1% each: $100 \times 1^2 = 100$ (very competitive)

Squaring gives big firms more weight. That's why the slide says HHI is better than CR4, the combined share of the top four firms. CR4 can't tell 25-25-25-25 apart from 85-5-5-5, but HHI can.

**How to read the numbers (US 2023 merger guidelines)**

| HHI | Meaning | Market on the slide |
|---|---|---|
| Below 1,000 | Unconcentrated | none |
| 1,000–1,800 | Moderately concentrated | Smartphones (1,150): many brands such as Samsung, Vivo, Xiaomi, Apple |
| Above 1,800 | Highly concentrated | Cabs, telecom, UPI (about 3,300–3,400): two or three big players. **Domestic aviation (5,012)** |
| Close to 10,000 | Near-monopoly | Web search (9,576): Google |

**Why this matters for your paper**
- The slide's aviation figure, **5,012** from DGCA data for June 2026, matches our own calculation. Our **ownership HHI for June 2026 is 5,011**, so the lecture independently backs up the paper's number.
- Our **brand HHI** for the same month is **4,724**. The gap of about 290 points comes from counting Air India and Air India Express as one group (one owner) rather than as separate brands. That gap is what the brand vs. ownership comparison (feedback #1 and O4) is about.
- Aviation is more than 2.5 times the 1,800 "highly concentrated" line. It is the most concentrated market on the slide after web search, and more concentrated than telecom, which most people think of as the classic Indian oligopoly.
- An HHI of about 5,000 means roughly the same concentration as two equal firms with 50% each. Aviation's two leaders are not equal, though: IndiGo has about 66% and the Air India Group about 24%. The paper calls this an asymmetric (lopsided) duopoly.

**For your O2 section:** the slide uses the 1,800 cut-off from the US 2023 guidelines. The same guidelines treat a rise of more than 100 points in a highly concentrated market as significant. Ownership HHI rose about 435 points after Jet's exit and about 686 points after Go First's exit, both far above that 100-point mark. That makes each exit a major concentration event, not just a transfer of passengers.

response.value:
This slide's point is that **knowing a market is concentrated doesn't tell you whether that's bad**. Three schools of thought read the same high HHI differently.

### Lens 1: Structure–Conduct–Performance (SCP)
**Idea:** Structure → Conduct → Performance. Few firms (structure) make it easy to avoid price wars or to collude (conduct), which leads to high prices and profits (performance).
**Simple version:** "Few firms = bad for customers."
**Policy:** watch HHI, block big mergers, break up dominant firms. India's MRTP Act (1969), the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, followed this logic. It was later replaced by the Competition Act 2002, under which CCI now works.

### Lens 2: Contestable markets
**Idea:** even a market with one or two firms can behave competitively if **outsiders could enter easily and leave without losing money**. The threat of entry keeps prices low.
**Key test: sunk costs**, meaning money you can't get back if you leave. With low sunk costs, a newcomer can "hit and run," so incumbents keep prices low.
**Example:** in 2016 telecom looked like a settled oligopoly. Jio entered and forced prices down sharply.

### Lens 3: Endogenous structure
**Idea:** concentration is often the **result** of competition, not its cause. Firms that invest better (in low costs, advertising, R&D or networks) win share, and the market becomes concentrated because they are better.
**Simple version:** "A few big firms may just mean a few efficient firms."
**Example:** IndiGo's cost leadership. Also, airlines like Jet and Go First still exited even though HHI was high. If high concentration guaranteed easy profits, as SCP suggests, they shouldn't have failed.

### How this connects to your paper

| Lens | Where it shows up |
|---|---|
| **SCP** | The trap the reviewer warned about in **feedback #7**: high HHI doesn't prove high fares. That's why the paper limits its claims to market structure, not market power. |
| **Contestable** | **CCI's reasoning** in the Vistara order: it approved the merger partly because low-cost airlines would keep the merged firm in check. That is a contestability argument. It also links to **O3**: did entrants like Akasa actually challenge the leaders? |
| **Endogenous** | **Your O2**: IndiGo took the largest share after each exit because it already had the aircraft, slots and low costs to absorb the passengers. Concentration rose because of who was able to expand. |

**Is aviation contestable?** Aircraft can be leased and moved, so they aren't fully sunk costs. But slots at busy airports, building a route network and early losses are sunk. So aviation is only **partly** contestable. That helps explain why exits mostly benefited the incumbents and not new entrants.

In December 2025, Indian domestic aviation faced a major operational crisis involving thousands of flight cancellations and widespread service disruptions \parencite{gupta2025antitrust}. A subsequent press release by the Ministry of Civil Aviation attributed the disruption to IndiGo’s over-optimisation of operations, inadequate regulatory preparedness, and failure to implement the revised Flight Duty Time Limitation (FDTL) provisions effectively \parencite{moca2026indigo,moca2024fatigue}. The ability of disruptions at a single airline to produce nationwide consequences points to the risks associated with the increasing concentration of India’s domestic passenger aviation market. Such concentration may reduce the number of effective alternatives available to passengers and increase the system-wide consequences of operational failures at a dominant carrier. Our study examines the Indian domestic aviation market from 2015 to 2026 to understand the key events that contributed to this concentration risk. We also explore the measures taken by the government to address these issues and improve the resilience of the domestic aviation market.

How did airline exits, acquisitions, and mergers alter ownership-adjusted market concentration in India's scheduled domestic passenger aviation market between January 2015 and July 2026, and do the resulting \HHI{} and \CRtwo{} measures indicate a transition from a multi-carrier oligopoly toward an asymmetric duopoly?

\item To track changes in the structure of the Indian domestic aviation market from January 2015 to July 2026 using monthly ownership-adjusted \HHI{}, \CRtwo{}, the number of active airline groups, and the market-share difference between the two largest groups.

\item To examine how passenger traffic, market share, and seat capacity were redistributed following the exits of Jet Airways and Go First and the consolidation of Air India, AIX Connect, and Vistara under the Tata Group, and to identify which airline groups gained the most from these changes.

\item To examine whether airlines entering the Indian domestic aviation market between 2015 and 2026 were able to grow into meaningful and persistent competitors by studying their market-share growth, survival duration, and eventual outcomes, including continued operation, exit, or merger.
\item To evaluate whether IndiGo and the Air India Group constitute an asymmetric duopoly and whether treating commonly owned brands separately understates concentration.

The study uses the course concept of \textbf{oligopoly} as its main theoretical framework. An oligopoly is characterised by a small number of major firms whose decisions are strategically interdependent. The \HHI{}, \CRtwo{}, number of active airline groups, and leader--rival market-share gap will be used as empirical measures of whether Indian domestic aviation moved from a multi-carrier oligopoly towards an asymmetric duopoly.

The course concepts of \textbf{barriers to entry} and \textbf{economies of scale and scope} will help explain why some entrants grew into meaningful competitors while others remained small or exited. \textbf{Market power} and \textbf{antitrust and competition policy} will guide the analysis of airline acquisitions, mergers, and common ownership, including whether separate airline brands overstate the number of independently controlled competitors.
% This section must synthesise sources across themes. Do not write a sequence
% of disconnected paper summaries; those belong in the annotated bibliography.
The reviewed literature falls into six thematic clusters, summarised in Table~\ref{tab:lit-clusters}.
Market Concentration & \textcite{kumari2026soaring}, \textcite{grosche2020concentration} & Market concentration, airline exits, compete or fix prices \\
New Entrants, Effective Competition & \textcite{oliveira2018effective} & New entrants, weak competition, big airlines stay on top \\
Budget Airlines, Fares, Demand & \textcite{wang2018determinants} & Budget airlines, lower fares, higher demand \\
Airline Finances, Survival & \textcite{jayathilakan2024determinants}, \textcite{ali2019impact} & Airline finances, survival, IndiGo vs Air India \\
Consolidation Events & \textcite{soman2024jet} (Jet), \textcite{jasrotia2025gofirst} (Go First), \textcite{chaudhary2023airindia} (AI--Vistara) & Airline exits, merger \\
Market Liberalisation, Privatisation & \textcite{findlay2004liberalization} & Market liberalisation, privatisation before 2015 \\

Taken together, the studies reviewed here each capture one part of the story, but none brings the parts into a single picture. Indian aviation was opened up to private competition before 2015 \parencite{findlay2004liberalization}. Budget-airline competition then lowered fares and helped IndiGo grow \parencite{wang2018determinants}. Financial performance diverged across carriers, with some remaining healthy while others weakened \parencite{jayathilakan2024determinants,ali2019impact}. The major structural events have each been documented separately: the exit of Jet Airways \parencite{soman2024jet}, the collapse of Go First \parencite{jasrotia2025gofirst}, and the Air India--Vistara merger \parencite{chaudhary2023airindia}. Comparative evidence shows that a single airline's collapse can raise concentration \parencite{grosche2020concentration}, and that new airlines often fail to become real competitors \parencite{oliveira2018effective}. The study closest to ours measures how concentrated Indian aviation is using standard indices such as \HHI{} and CR4 \parencite{kumari2026soaring}.
Despite these contributions, the literature lacks an integrated, longitudinal analysis of the Indian scheduled domestic passenger market that simultaneously addresses three dimensions:

\item No study systematically links the sequence of dated exits, acquisitions and mergers between 2015 and 2026 to the corresponding movements in market concentration, treating these events collectively rather than as isolated cases;

\item Existing concentration measures are constructed at the level of operating brands and do not account for common ownership, even though Air India, Air India Express, Vistara and AirAsia India came under the single control of the Tata-owned Air India Group; and
\item Prior work does not establish whether the observed shift toward an IndiGo and Air India Group duopoly represents a durable structural change or a transitory phase.
This study addresses these three gaps.

In light of the reviewed literature, which documents these developments only in isolation, the study restates its central question as follows: how did the sequence of airline exits, the Tata Group's acquisition of Air India, and the 2024 brand mergers reshape monthly concentration in India's scheduled domestic passenger market between January 2015 and July 2026 once commonly owned brands are grouped by ownership, and do the resulting \HHI{}, \CRtwo{}, and effective number of competitors indicate a durable rather than transitory shift from a multi-carrier oligopoly toward an asymmetric IndiGo--Air India Group duopoly?
% The three-page concept note ends here. The annotated bibliography below is

To answer this question, the study needs monthly airline-level statistics for the Indian scheduled domestic passenger market from January 2015 to July 2026: for each airline and month, passengers carried, passenger- and seat-kilometres, and the passenger load factor, together with an ownership classification that groups commonly controlled brands (for example, Air India, Air India Express, Vistara and AirAsia India under the Tata-owned Air India Group) and dated records of the major exits, the Air India acquisition, and the 2024 mergers. These come from a cleaned, openly licensed distribution of DGCA traffic workbooks. Fare, profit, consumer-welfare, delay, and service-quality data are not required and are excluded, because no reliable public series exists for them over this period.

|---|---|

I'm drafting different phrasings for the research objective, comparing a fuller version examining airline entrants' market-share growth, survival, and outcomes against a shorter version that moves methodological detail into separate variables.

No feedback actually flagged O3, but it was shortened during drafting for brevity rather than substance—losing words like "meaningful" and the specifics on growth/survival/outcomes—so I'm leaning toward restoring the fuller wording. I'm also mapping overlap with O2: Akasa Air's 2022 entry absorbed a chunk of Go First's share, making it both an O2 event and an O3 entrant case, while other entrants that exited (TruJet, Zoom Air, etc.) are purely O3 outcomes. The key distinction is that O2 is event-centered around what happens at an exit, while O3 is firm-centered, tracking each newcomer's trajectory over time—so the two questions are complementary rather than redundant.

I'm checking Akasa's exact numbers: it launched August 2022, with pre-entry share of 1.64% rising to 4.495% post, meaning it captured about 35.3% of Go First's vacated share, though some of that reflects Akasa's own ramp-up trend rather than purely Go First's exit. Smaller exits like TruJet, Zoom Air, Air Costa, and Air Pegasus fall outside O2's scope since that only covers the major Jet Airways and Go First exits. My plan is to restore the fuller O3 wording and add an explicit boundary sentence clarifying that O2 captures Akasa's share gain as part of Go First's decomposition while O3 handles Akasa's full trajectory, avoiding double-counting.

**Why O3 got shorter:** nothing changed in substance. When the Assignment 2 draft was set up, all four objectives were cut to one line each to save space in a 2–3 page document. The detail moved elsewhere:

| Assignment 1 O3 wording | Where it is now in Assignment 2 |
|---|---|
| "market-share growth, survival duration" | Variables table, "Entrant outcomes" row (peak share, months in operation) |
| "eventual outcomes: continued operation, exit, or merger" | Same row ("final status") and the O3 method section |
| "meaningful and persistent competitors" | Shortened to just "persistent competitors" |

No feedback point applies to O3, so there was no reason to change it. The shortening did drop "meaningful", and the objective now reads thinner than O1, O2 and O4. I'd put back the Assignment 1 wording:

> **O3.** Examine whether airlines entering the market after 2015 grew into meaningful and persistent competitors, using their market-share growth, survival and eventual outcome (still operating, exited or merged).

**Does O3 overlap with O2?** They're different questions, but they meet at one point: **Akasa Air**.

| | **O2** | **O3** |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | Events: what happened when a big airline left | Firms: the full life of each new airline |
| **Question** | Where did Jet Airways' and Go First's share go? | Did newcomers become real rivals? |
| **Airlines** | All groups, in fixed windows around two exits | Only entrants since 2015 (Akasa, Star Air, Flybig, TruJet, Fly91…) |

**Where they meet:**
- **Akasa** started flying in August 2022. In your Go First decomposition, it gained about 2.9 percentage points, roughly 35% of Go First's passenger share. So an O3 airline shows up in O2's results.
- Some entrants also exited (TruJet, Zoom Air). Those exits belong to O3, not O2, because O2 covers only the two major exits.

**How to keep them separate:** O2 reports Akasa's gain only inside the Go First window, and says it partly reflects Akasa's own growth (already in your "own trends" challenge). O3 covers Akasa's full path and whether it became a lasting competitor. Each part can then point to the other: O2's results show whether entrants could take the share that exits freed up, and O3's results show whether they kept it.

Should I restore the fuller O3 wording (gray) and add one black sentence to your O2 method section explaining how it relates to O3?

### O2 vs O3 in one line each

- **O2 looks at airlines that left.** When a big airline shut down, who got its passengers?
- **O3 looks at airlines that arrived.** When a new airline started, did it grow and survive?

### A shop example

Picture a market street.
- **O2:** two big shops close (Jet Airways, Go First). You ask: "Which shops got their customers?" You look at the year before and the year after each closure.
- **O3:** new shops keep opening (Akasa, Star Air, Flybig, TruJet). You ask: "Did any of them become a serious rival, or did they stay tiny or close?" You follow each new shop from the day it opened.

### Side by side

| | **O2 (yours)** | **O3** |
|---|---|---|
| Starts from | An exit or a merger | An airline's first flight |
| Airlines studied | Everyone, in the window around the exit | Only airlines that entered after 2015 |
| Time looked at | About 12 months before and after each event | From an airline's first flight to now (or until it closed) |
| Answer looks like | "IndiGo took 66% of Go First's share" | "Akasa reached about 6%, still flying. TruJet peaked under 1%, exited" |

### The one place they meet

Akasa shows up in both, but answers a different question in each.
- **In O2:** "Akasa gained about 35% of Go First's share in the year after Go First left." That is one snapshot.
- **In O3:** "Akasa grew from 0 to about 6% since 2022 and is still flying." That is its whole story.

### O2 vs O3 in one line each

- **O2 looks at airlines that left.** When a big airline shut down, who got its passengers?
- **O3 looks at airlines that arrived.** When a new airline started, did it grow and survive?

### A shop example

Picture a market street.
- **O2:** two big shops close (Jet Airways, Go First). You ask: "Which shops got their customers?" You look at the year before and the year after each closure.
- **O3:** new shops keep opening (Akasa, Star Air, Flybig, TruJet). You ask: "Did any of them become a serious rival, or did they stay tiny or close?" You follow each new shop from the day it opened.

|---|---|---|

**Research question**
> How did exits, acquisitions and mergers between 2015 and 2026 change concentration in India's scheduled domestic aviation market when airlines with the same owner are counted as one firm, and has the market moved from an oligopoly of several airlines to a lasting asymmetric duopoly, based on set thresholds?

**Objectives**
- **O1.** To measure monthly concentration using brand-level, ownership-level and modified HHI along with CR2, and to estimate how much each exit and merger changed it. Since we have no fare data, we limit our claims to market structure.
- **O2.** To find out which airlines took over the passengers and seats left by Jet Airways (2019) and Go First (2023), whether access to slots and aircraft explains this, and how the Tata Group's consolidation compares with CCI's own merger review.
- **O3.** To check whether airlines that entered after 2015 managed to grow and stay in the market, by looking at their market share over time, how long they lasted and how they ended up (still flying, shut down or merged).
- **O4.** To test whether the market meets set duopoly thresholds for CR2, HHI, share gap and fringe share, to see whether national figures hide single-airline routes among the top 20–30 routes (if city-pair data is available), and to measure rivals' spare capacity in December 2025 and the capacity share where IndiGo is the only or main operator.

**What changed:**
- Replaced polished phrasing with everyday words: "reshape" → "change", "narrowed into a durable" → "moved … to a lasting", "absorbed" → "took over", "persistent competitors" → "grow and stay in the market", "pre-defined" → "set".
- Wrote "airlines with the same owner are counted as one firm" instead of the abstract "once common ownership is taken into account".
- Made the no-fare-data point its own short sentence in O1, as a person would add it.
- Dropped the effective number of firms from O1 to shorten it. It is still in the variables table.

**About AI detectors:** these tools are unreliable and often flag human writing too. Rewording a few sentences won't change a detector's result much. The surest way to sound like your team is to read each sentence aloud and rephrase anything that doesn't sound like how you'd explain it. The paper also has an AI-use section, carried over from Assignment 1. Keep it accurate about how AI was used, so that whatever a detector says, your own statement already covers it.

response.value:
That clause means: **compare what our data shows about the Tata mergers with what the regulator (CCI) said when it approved them.**

**1. "The Tata Group consolidation (2022–2024)"**
Tata brought several airlines under one owner in steps:
- **January 2022:** Tata took over Air India and Air India Express. It already co-owned Vistara and AirAsia India.
- **2024:** AirAsia India (renamed AIX Connect) merged into Air India Express, and Vistara merged into Air India.

So four brands became one group, the Air India Group.

**2. "CCI's combination order"**
In India, a big merger needs approval from the **Competition Commission of India (CCI)**. When CCI approved the Air India–Vistara merger in September 2023, it published a document explaining its decision. That document is the "combination order".

**3. "Assess … against"**
Put the two side by side:

| | CCI's view (2023) | Our data |
|---|---|---|
| **What it looked at** | Individual routes (48 where both airlines flew) | The whole national market |
| **What it concluded** | Merger is fine, with conditions on 7 routes | Ownership HHI rose with each Tata step |
| **Why it was comfortable** | Low-cost rivals would keep the merged airline in check | Did those rivals stay strong? The share held by airlines outside IndiGo and the Air India Group fell from about 19% to about 10% after approval. |

**In plain words:** CCI said the merger was safe because other airlines would keep competing. We check whether that turned out to be true, using our numbers.

That's also the reviewer's point in #6: base the competition-policy discussion on the regulator's actual decision, not on news reports.

Our data has one row per **airline per month**, for example "IndiGo, June 2023: 8.2 million passengers". That is the **airline-month**, the building block.

airline-month rows  →  added up  →  market-month (HHI, CR2)
(IndiGo Jun-23,                      (Jun-23: HHI 4,650)
 Air India Jun-23, …)

| **O4** | Market-month (route-month if city-pair data is found) | "Every month since Dec 2024 meets the thresholds?" |

response.value:
Right. The CCI order **doesn't belong in the unit of analysis**. Here's why, and one small fix the O2 row does need.

**Unit of analysis ≠ data sources**
- **Unit of analysis** = what one row of *your numbers* describes. O2's numbers all come from the DGCA airline-month data.
- **The CCI order and the company filings** are *documents* you read and quote. They give no rows to count, so they have no unit. They belong in **Section 3 (Data sources)**, where both are already listed, and in your **method section (§5.2)**, where they're already used.

**The fix: the O2 row only covers half of O2**
O2 has two parts, and each uses a slightly different unit:

| O2 part | Unit | Source of numbers |
|---|---|---|
| Exits (#5) | Ownership group, before vs. after each exit | DGCA airline-month |
| Tata consolidation (#6) | **Market-month**, before vs. after each Tata step (brand vs. ownership HHI) | DGCA airline-month |

Right now the row only says "before vs. after each exit". I'd change it to:

> **O2:** Ownership group before vs. after each exit; market-month before vs. after each Tata consolidation step

Should I make that change?

rebuilt cleanly at 10 pages. Before writing it in, I recomputed it from our data, and it reproduces the HHI changes we already had.

### Part 1: Exits (#5)

**1. Average share before and after the exit** (exit month left out):
$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^k|}\sum_{t\in W^k} s_{gt}, \qquad \Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$
In words: take each airline group's average share in the year before the exit and the year after, then subtract.

**2. Absorption ratio: who took what portion of the exiting airline's share**
$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}}\times 100, \qquad \sum_{g\neq x} a_g = 100\%$$
In words: divide each group's gain by the exiting airline's old share. All the portions add up to 100%. A negative value means that group lost share.

**3. Contribution to the rise in HHI: whose gain made the market more concentrated**
$$\Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g, \qquad c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2$$
In words: the same gain raises HHI more when it goes to a group that is already big. This is the part that turns "who gained" into "whose gain raised concentration".

**4. Passengers vs. seat-km:** if a group's absorption ratio for seat-km is higher than for passengers, it added aircraft and flights faster than it gained travellers. That is the link to the slot and fleet evidence in the filings.

### Part 2: Consolidation (#6)

**5. Mechanical merger ΔHHI**
$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a\, s_b$$
In words: when brands come under one owner, HHI rises immediately even though no passenger moves. This formula gives that rise from the brands' shares in the month before the event. It is the standard antitrust merger formula.

**6. Observed vs. mechanical:** compare the actual change in ownership HHI with this mechanical figure. The difference is how much the market itself moved after the merger.

**7. Testing CCI's assumption:** the fringe share is $F_t = 100 - \text{CR2}_t$. Compare its average in FY2022–23 with its average after September 2023.

| Jet exit | +444 | +435 | IndiGo contributes +473, more than the whole change |
| Go First exit | +690 | +686 | IndiGo contributes +631, about 92% of the rise |
| Tata, January 2022 | Mechanical +334 | Observed +373 | About 40 points come from how the market moved afterwards |

Your O2 method section (§5.2) now has a small mathematical model for both parts. It's all in black, and [main.pdf](term-paper/assignment-2/main.pdf) rebuilt cleanly at 10 pages. Before writing it in, I recomputed it from our data, and it reproduces the HHI changes we already had.

### Part 1: Exits (#5)

**1. Average share before and after the exit** (exit month left out):
$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^k|}\sum_{t\in W^k} s_{gt}, \qquad \Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$
In words: take each airline group's average share in the year before the exit and the year after, then subtract.

**2. Absorption ratio: who took what portion of the exiting airline's share**
$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}}\times 100, \qquad \sum_{g\neq x} a_g = 100\%$$
In words: divide each group's gain by the exiting airline's old share. All the portions add up to 100%. A negative value means that group lost share.

**3. Contribution to the rise in HHI: whose gain made the market more concentrated**
$$\Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g, \qquad c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2$$
In words: the same gain raises HHI more when it goes to a group that is already big. This is the part that turns "who gained" into "whose gain raised concentration".

**4. Passengers vs. seat-km:** if a group's absorption ratio for seat-km is higher than for passengers, it added aircraft and flights faster than it gained travellers. That is the link to the slot and fleet evidence in the filings.

### Part 2: Consolidation (#6)

**5. Mechanical merger ΔHHI**
$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a\, s_b$$
In words: when brands come under one owner, HHI rises immediately even though no passenger moves. This formula gives that rise from the brands' shares in the month before the event. It is the standard antitrust merger formula.

**6. Observed vs. mechanical:** compare the actual change in ownership HHI with this mechanical figure. The difference is how much the market itself moved after the merger.

\subsection{O2: Who gained from exits and consolidation}

\textbf{Exits (feedback \#5).} For each exit, compare every ownership group's mean share before and after, for passengers and for seat-km, leaving out the exit month. The windows are April 2018--March 2019 vs.\ May 2019--February 2020 for Jet Airways (cut before COVID) and May 2022--April 2023 vs.\ June 2023--May 2024 for Go First. Seat-km shows who added aircraft and flights, and passengers show who carried the travellers. The shifts are then linked to company filings. SpiceJet reports 74 slots allotted and 31 aircraft inducted after a full-service carrier stopped flying in 2019 \parencite[p.~62]{spicejet2020annual}, and Go Airlines reports engine-related groundings before its exit \parencite[p.~35]{goair2021drhp}.

\textbf{Consolidation (feedback \#6).} When brands come under one owner no passengers move, so the question is how far concentration rises. Compare brand and ownership \HHI{} in 12-month windows around the January 2022 acquisition and the December 2024 mergers, and set this against the regulator's own decision. CCI approved the Air India--Vistara merger on 1 September 2023 after a route-by-route review of 48 overlapping domestic city pairs, with capacity commitments on seven routes \parencite[paras.~19, 115--127]{cci2023vistara}. It relied on rivals' slot holdings and on ``competition from LCCs with much lower cost bases'' (paras.~109, 111), using FY2022--23 data from before Go First stopped flying in May 2023. The Go First decomposition and the fringe share after approval show whether that low-cost competition persisted.

\textbf{Justification.} Two exits and two consolidation steps are too few for a regression. A before-and-after decomposition shows directly where the share went, the filings explain why, and the CCI order grounds the policy discussion in the regulator's actual reasoning rather than secondary reports.

**Meaning:** add up a group's monthly shares in the window and divide by the number of months. That's just an average.

- $g$ = airline group (IndiGo, Air India Group, …)
- $t$ = month
- $W^{\text{pre}}$ = May 2022 – Apr 2023 (12 months before)
- $W^{\text{post}}$ = Jun 2023 – May 2024 (12 months after; May 2023 itself is left out)

| Group | $\bar s^{\,\text{pre}}$ | $\bar s^{\,\text{post}}$ |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 56.6% | 61.9% |
| Air India Group | 24.6% | 27.3% |
| Go First ($x$) | 8.1% | 0% |
| SpiceJet | 7.6% | 4.9% |
| Akasa Air | 1.6% | 4.5% |

### Line 2: Change in share
$$\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$

**Meaning:** after minus before.

| Group | $\Delta s_g$ |
|---|---|
| IndiGo | 61.9 − 56.6 = **+5.3 pp** |
| Air India Group | **+2.7 pp** |
| Akasa | **+2.9 pp** |
| SpiceJet | **−2.7 pp** |

### Line 3: Absorption ratio
$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}} \times 100, \qquad \sum_{g \neq x} a_g = 100\%$$

**Meaning:** what portion of Go First's old 8.1% each group picked up.

| Group | Working | $a_g$ |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 5.33 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **66%** |
| Akasa | 2.86 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **35%** |
| Air India Group | 2.72 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **34%** |
| SpiceJet | −2.72 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **−34%** |
| Others (tiny) | | about −1% |
| **Total** | | **100%** |

**Why the total is 100%:** shares always add up to 100. When Go First's 8.1% disappears, everyone else's changes must add up to exactly 8.1%. A **negative** ratio means that group *lost* share. SpiceJet shrank even though a rival left, so IndiGo, Akasa and the Air India Group together took more than 100% of Go First's share.

### Line 4: Contribution to the rise in HHI
$$\Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g \neq x} c_g, \qquad c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2$$

**Meaning:** HHI is the sum of squared shares. When a share changes from $s$ to $s+\Delta$, its square changes by $(s+\Delta)^2 - s^2 = 2s\Delta + \Delta^2$. That is $c_g$.

| Part | Working | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Go First disappears | −(8.08)² | **−65** |
| IndiGo | 2 × 56.6 × 5.33 + 5.33² | **+631** |
| Air India Group | 2 × 24.6 × 2.72 + 2.72² | **+141** |
| Akasa | 2 × 1.6 × 2.86 + 2.86² | **+18** |
| SpiceJet | 2 × 7.6 × (−2.72) + 2.72² | **−34** |
| **Total ΔHHI** | | **≈ +690** |

**The key insight:** Akasa gained about as much share as the Air India Group (+2.9 vs. +2.7 pp) but added only 18 HHI points, against 141 for the Air India Group. **A gain going to an already big firm raises concentration much more.** IndiGo alone caused about 92% of the rise (631 of 690).

### Line 5: Passengers vs. seat-km
> "Both are computed for passengers and seat-km. A higher seat-km ratio indicates capacity-led expansion…"

Run the same absorption ratio using seat-km (capacity) instead of passengers:

| Group | $a_g$ passengers | $a_g$ seat-km | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Akasa | 35% | **41%** | Added planes and flights faster than it filled them: **capacity-led** |
| Air India Group | **34%** | 30% | Filled existing seats: **demand-led** |
| IndiGo | 66% | 66% | Both grew together |

**Why it matters:** capacity-led growth needs aircraft and slots. Those cases are the ones you check against the filings, as with SpiceJet's 74 slots and 31 aircraft after the Jet exit.

## Part 2: Consolidation

### Line 6: Mechanical merger ΔHHI
$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b;\; a,b \in G} s_a\, s_b$$

**Meaning:** when separate brands get one owner, nobody switches airline, but HHI jumps because the shares are now counted together. If two firms have $s_a$ and $s_b$, combining them gives $(s_a+s_b)^2 = s_a^2 + s_b^2 + 2s_as_b$. The extra part is $2s_as_b$.

Tata, January 2022, shares in December 2021:

| Brand | Share |
|---|---|
| Air India (with AI Express, already grouped) | 8.5% |
| Vistara | 7.7% |
| AirAsia India | 6.3% |

$$2 \times (8.5 \times 7.7 \;+\; 8.5 \times 6.3 \;+\; 7.7 \times 6.3) \approx 2 \times 167 = \textbf{+334 points}$$

> "The observed change in ownership HHI … is compared with this."

| | Points |
|---|---|

| Observed (12 months after vs. before) | +373 |
| **Difference** | **+39** |

**Reading:** most of the jump comes simply from the change of owner. The extra 39 points show the market kept concentrating afterwards, partly as demand recovered from COVID.

**Meaning:** the fringe share is everything outside the top two (IndiGo and the Air India Group). CCI approved the merger partly because low-cost rivals would keep competing. If the fringe shrinks after approval, that assumption weakened.

| Period | Mean fringe share |
|---|---|
| FY2022–23 (the data CCI used) | **19.2%** |
| After CCI's approval (Oct 2023 – Jul 2026) | **9.6%** |

**Reading:** the competition CCI counted on roughly halved, largely because Go First exited and SpiceJet shrank.

Exit happens → average shares before/after (L1) → change (L2)
            → who took what portion (L3) → whose gain raised HHI (L4)
            → capacity-led or demand-led? (L5) → check filings

Merger happens → expected HHI jump from ownership alone (L6)
              → compare with actual jump (L7)
              → did CCI's "low-cost rivals" assumption hold? (L8)
```

### 1. Why would passengers be zero?

I checked: 132 scheduled-domestic rows have 0 passengers. There are three reasons:

| Reason | Airlines | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| **Cargo airlines** listed in the domestic table but carrying only cargo | Blue Dart Aviation, QuikJet Cargo | 111 |
| **Small airlines in months they weren't flying** (suspended, or before a restart) | Zoom Air, Air Pegasus, Air Odisha, Air Deccan | 17 |
| **Airlines still listed just after shutting down** | Jet Airways and JetLite, May–June 2019 | 4 |

These rows have to go. Cargo airlines aren't in the passenger market, and a 0 for Jet in May 2019 would wrongly make Jet look like a firm that is still "in the market". April 2020 (lockdown) isn't in the raw file at all, so it simply has no rows.

### 2. Seat-km, passenger-km and PLF

Picture one flight: a **180-seat** plane flies **Delhi → Mumbai (about 1,150 km)** with **150 passengers** on board.

| Measure | Meaning | Formula | This flight |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Passengers** | People carried | count | 150 |
| **Seat-km** (ASK) | **Capacity offered**: every seat, full or empty, times distance | seats × km | 180 × 1,150 = **207,000** |
| **Passenger-km** (RPK) | **Capacity actually used**: only occupied seats, times distance | passengers × km | 150 × 1,150 = **172,500** |
| **PLF** (passenger load factor) | **How full the planes were** | passenger-km ÷ seat-km × 100 | 172,500 ÷ 207,000 = **83.3%** |

**Why distance is multiplied in:** a seat on a 2,000 km flight is more capacity than a seat on a 300 km flight. Seat-km measures capacity fairly across short and long routes.

**In the data:** `seat_km` and `passenger_km` are in **thousands**, added up over all of an airline's flights in that month.

**Why O2 uses both passengers and seat-km:**
- **Passengers** show who *carried the travellers*.
- **Seat-km** show who *added planes and flights*.

When an airline's seat-km share rises faster than its passenger share, it expanded capacity first. That's the link to slots and aircraft.

## From raw data to the O2 formulas

### Stage A: Raw data → clean data
**File:**

(3,482 rows: every airline, every month, every service type)

**Step 1. Keep only scheduled domestic flights.**
Drop rows where `service_type` is international or non-scheduled (charter).

**Step 2. Drop rows with zero passengers.**
That removes 132 rows: cargo airlines (Blue Dart, QuikJet), small airlines in months they weren't flying, and Jet Airways just after its shutdown.

**Step 3. Build a date.**

becomes the first day of that month, e.g. 2023 + 6 → 2023-06-01.

**Step 4. Keep the columns we need.**

, `seat_km`, `passenger_km`, `plf`.

**Step 5. Add an ownership group.**
- Jet Airways + JetLite → Jet Airways Group (always)
- Air India + Air India Express → Air India Group (always)
- Vistara, AirAsia India, AIX Connect → Air India Group (from January 2022)
- Everyone else → their own name

**Result:**

, 1,577 rows (one per airline per month), January 2015 – July 2026.

### Stage B: Clean data → exit decomposition
**Step 6. Calculate monthly shares** (separately for passengers and seat-km):
$$s_{gt} = \frac{\text{group } g\text{'s total in month } t}{\text{market total in month } t} \times 100$$

**Step 7. Set the windows (exit month left out).**
| Exit | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Jet Airways | Apr 2018 – Mar 2019 | May 2019 – Feb 2020 |
| Go First | May 2022 – Apr 2023 | Jun 2023 – May 2024 |

**Step 8. Average share in each window** (formula L1):
$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^k|}\sum_{t\in W^k} s_{gt}$$
This gives `pre_share` and `post_share`. Months when a group didn't exist count as 0.

**Step 9. Change in share** (L2):
$$\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$
This gives `change_pp`.

**Step 10. Absorption ratio** (L3):
$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}}\times 100$$
This gives `pct_of_exiting_share`. For all groups except the one that exited, the ratios add up to 100%.

**Result:**

### Stage C: Extra calculations from the formulas (not yet saved in any file)
**Step 11. Contribution to ΔHHI** (L4), using `pre_share` and `change_pp`:
$$c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2, \qquad \Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g$$

**Step 12. Passengers vs. seat-km** (L5):
Compare $a_g$ for `passengers_share` with $a_g$ for `seat_km_share`. If seat-km is higher, the airline grew through capacity, so check the slot and fleet evidence in the filings.

**Step 13. Mechanical merger ΔHHI** (L6), from the clean data for December 2021:
$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a s_b \quad \text{(Air India, Vistara, AirAsia India)}$$

**Step 14. Observed vs. mechanical** (L7):
Compare with `change_ownership_hhi` in [event_window_comparisons.csv](term-paper/analysis/data/processed/event_window_comparisons.csv).

**Step 15. Fringe share** (L8), from [monthly_market_concentration.csv](term-paper/analysis/data/processed/monthly_market_concentration.csv):
$$F_t = 100 - \text{CR2}_t$$
Average it over FY2022–23 and over the months after CCI's approval, then compare.

O2 results (for Assignment 3)

**Step 8. Average share in each window** (formula L1):
$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^k|}\sum_{t\in W^k} s_{gt}$$
This gives `pre_share` and `post_share`. Months when a group didn't exist count as 0.

**Step 9. Change in share** (L2):
$$\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$
This gives `change_pp`.

**Step 10. Absorption ratio** (L3):
$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}}\times 100$$
This gives `pct_of_exiting_share`. For all groups except the one that exited, the ratios add up to 100%.

**Result:** [exit_share_decomposition.csv](term-paper/analysis/data/processed/exit_share_decomposition.csv)

### Stage C: Extra calculations from the formulas (not yet saved in any file)
**Step 11. Contribution to ΔHHI** (L4), using `pre_share` and `change_pp`:
$$c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2, \qquad \Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g$$

**Step 12. Passengers vs. seat-km** (L5):
Compare $a_g$ for `passengers_share` with $a_g$ for `seat_km_share`. If seat-km is higher, the airline grew through capacity, so check the slot and fleet evidence in the filings.

**Step 13. Mechanical merger ΔHHI** (L6), from the clean data for December 2021:
$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a s_b \quad \text{(Air India, Vistara, AirAsia India)}$$

**Step 14. Observed vs. mechanical** (L7):
Compare with `change_ownership_hhi` in [event_window_comparisons.csv](term-paper/analysis/data/processed/event_window_comparisons.csv).

**Step 15. Fringe share** (L8), from [monthly_market_concentration.csv](term-paper/analysis/data/processed/monthly_market_concentration.csv):
$$F_t = 100 - \text{CR2}_t$$
Average it over FY2022–23 and over the months after CCI's approval, then compare.

  │  Steps 1–5: filter, date, ownership group

clean_scheduled_domestic.csv (1,577 rows)
  │  Steps 6–10: monthly shares → window averages → change → absorption

```

response.value:
Yes, and the data confirms it: all 1,577 rows in the clean file have passenger-km ≤ seat-km. One correction to how you described seat-km, though.

**Seat-km is not just the number of seats.** It's **seats × distance flown**, so it measures capacity in both seats and kilometres:

| | What it counts | Example (180 seats, 150 passengers, 1,150 km) |
|---|---|---|
| **Seat-km** | Every seat offered, full or empty, × km | 180 × 1,150 = 207,000 |
| **Passenger-km** | Only occupied seats × km | 150 × 1,150 = 172,500 |

**Why passenger-km ≤ seat-km:** you can't carry more passengers than you have seats. The best case is a completely full plane, where they're equal.

That's also why **PLF = passenger-km ÷ seat-km × 100** always falls between 0% and 100%.

The gap between the two (seat-km − passenger-km) is **empty seat-km**, the unused capacity. That's the "rivals' spare capacity" measure from feedback #4 in O4.

## Step 6: Calculate monthly shares

**The question it answers:** "In a given month, what percentage of all domestic passengers did each airline group carry?"

### A real example: June 2023

**Part 1. Start from the clean data.** There's one row per airline for that month:

| Airline | Ownership group | Passengers |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | IndiGo | 7,893,296 |
| Air India | Air India Group | 1,212,719 |
| Vistara | Air India Group | 1,011,426 |
| AirAsia India | Air India Group | 1,003,619 |
| Akasa Air | Akasa Air | 618,053 |
| SpiceJet | SpiceJet | 555,248 |
| Alliance Air | Alliance Air | 144,033 |
| Star Air, Flybig, India One Air | (each their own) | 48,207 together |

**Part 2. Add up the whole market.**
Total passengers in June 2023 = **12,486,601**

**Part 3. Add up each ownership group.**
Air India, Vistara and AirAsia India all belong to the Air India Group, so they're combined:
1,212,719 + 1,011,426 + 1,003,619 = **3,227,764**

**Part 4. Divide each group by the total and multiply by 100.**

| Group | Working | Share $s_{gt}$ |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 7,893,296 ÷ 12,486,601 × 100 | **63.2%** |
| Air India Group | 3,227,764 ÷ 12,486,601 × 100 | **25.9%** |
| Akasa Air | 618,053 ÷ 12,486,601 × 100 | **4.9%** |
| SpiceJet | 555,248 ÷ 12,486,601 × 100 | **4.4%** |
| Alliance Air | 144,033 ÷ 12,486,601 × 100 | **1.2%** |
| Others | | **0.4%** |
| **Total** | | **100%** |

### The formula
$$s_{gt} = \frac{\text{group } g\text{'s passengers in month } t}{\text{all passengers in month } t} \times 100$$

- $g$ = the group (e.g. IndiGo)
- $t$ = the month (e.g. June 2023)
- $s_{gt}$ = that group's share in that month (e.g. 63.2%)

### Repeat it
The script does this for **every month** from January 2015 to July 2026, and **twice**:
- once with **passengers**, giving passenger share;
- once with **seat-km**, giving capacity share (same steps, using the `seat_km` column).

**Why shares and not raw passenger counts:** the market grows over time. IndiGo carrying more passengers in 2024 than in 2022 doesn't mean it gained ground, because everyone may have grown. A share shows whether it gained **relative to the others**, and that's what concentration is about.

Next, Step 7 picks which months to compare.

response.value:
## Step 7: Set the windows

**The question it answers:** "Which months count as *before* the exit and which count as *after*?"

Step 6 gave a share for every month. To see what changed because of an exit, you compare a stretch of normal months **before** with a stretch of normal months **after**. Each stretch is a **window**.

### The windows

| Exit | Before window ($W^{\text{pre}}$) | Left out | After window ($W^{\text{post}}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Jet Airways** (stopped 17 April 2019) | Apr 2018 – Mar 2019 (12 months) | **Apr 2019** | May 2019 – Feb 2020 (10 months) |
| **Go First** (stopped 3 May 2023) | May 2022 – Apr 2023 (12 months) | **May 2023** | Jun 2023 – May 2024 (12 months) |

### Decision 1: Why use a window, not a single month?
Single months jump around because of holidays, weather, festival travel and so on. An average over about a year smooths that out and also covers every season once.

### Decision 2: Why leave out the exit month?
In the exit month the airline flew for part of the month only, so that month is neither "before" nor "after". The data shows this:

| Month | Go First share | IndiGo share |
|---|---|---|
| Apr 2023 | 6.4% | 57.5% |
| **May 2023** | **0.4%** (flew only 2 days) | **61.4%** |
| Jun 2023 | 0% | 63.2% |

Counting May 2023 in either window would blur the comparison.

### Decision 3: Why does the Jet "after" window stop at February 2020?
COVID:

| Month | Total domestic passengers |
|---|---|
| Feb 2020 | 12.3 million |
| Mar 2020 | 7.7 million (lockdown begins) |
| May 2020 | 0.3 million |

If the window ran into March 2020, the share changes would mix up **Jet's exit** with **the pandemic**. So it stops at February 2020, giving 10 months instead of 12.

### A limitation to know
Jet didn't disappear overnight. It was already shrinking before it stopped:

| Month | Jet share |
|---|---|
| Feb 2019 | 11.4% |
| Mar 2019 | 5.7% |
| Apr 2019 | 0.9% |

So the "before" window (Apr 2018 – Mar 2019) already includes some of the decline. Part of the shift to rivals had started before April 2019, and the decomposition may slightly *understate* how much others gained. This belongs in Assignment 3's limitations, and could be tested by ending the before window in December 2018.

### What comes out of Step 7
Just two lists of months per exit, the before months and the after months. Step 8 then averages each group's monthly shares over those months.

## Step 9: Change in share

**The question it answers:** "How much did each group's share go up or down after the exit?"

### Formula
$$\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$

In words: **after minus before.** ($\Delta$, "delta", means "change in".)

### Example: Go First exit, passenger shares

| Group | Before $\bar s^{\text{pre}}$ | After $\bar s^{\text{post}}$ | Change $\Delta s_g$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 56.56 | 61.89 | **+5.33** |
| Akasa Air | 1.64 | 4.50 | **+2.86** |
| Air India Group | 24.55 | 27.27 | **+2.72** |
| Star Air | 0.17 | 0.31 | +0.15 |
| Fly91, India One Air | 0.01 | 0.02 | +0.02 |
| Flybig | 0.19 | 0.08 | −0.11 |
| Alliance Air | 1.17 | 1.01 | −0.16 |
| SpiceJet | 7.64 | 4.91 | **−2.72** |
| **Go First** (exited) | 8.08 | 0 | **−8.08** |
| **Sum of all changes** | | | **0** |

### Two things to notice

**1. All the changes add up to zero.**
Shares always total 100% before and after, so whatever one group loses, others must gain. Go First's −8.08 is balanced exactly by everyone else:
- gains: +5.33 + 2.86 + 2.72 + 0.15 + 0.02 = **+11.08**
- other losses: −2.72 − 0.16 − 0.11 = **−2.99**
- net for the others: 11.08 − 2.99 = **+8.08**, exactly Go First's old share.

That's why Step 10's absorption ratios add up to 100%.

**2. "pp" means percentage points, not percent.**
IndiGo went from 56.56% to 61.89%, a change of **+5.33 percentage points (pp)**. That isn't "+5.33%". In percent terms, IndiGo's share grew by 5.33 ÷ 56.56 ≈ 9.4%. We always report changes in **pp**.

### Same step for the Jet Airways exit (for comparison)

| Group | Change $\Delta s_g$ |
|---|---|
| IndiGo | +5.21 |
| SpiceJet | **+3.16** |
| Vistara | +1.97 |
| Go First | +1.95 |
| AirAsia India | +1.47 |
| Air India Group | −0.14 |
| **Jet Airways Group** (exited) | **−13.82** |

**Interesting contrast:**
- After Jet (2019), **SpiceJet gained** +3.2 pp. It took Jet's slots and planes, as its annual report says.
- After Go First (2023), **SpiceJet lost** −2.7 pp. It was struggling itself by then.

The same airline was a winner in one exit and a loser in the other. That's the kind of point the slot and fleet evidence helps explain.

### What comes out of Step 9
One number per group per exit: `change_pp` in
. Step 10 turns it into a percentage of the exiting airline's share.

## Step 10: Absorption ratio

**The question it answers:** "Of the share the exiting airline left behind, what *portion* did each group take?"

Step 9 gave changes in percentage points, but the exits were different sizes (Jet held 13.8%, Go First 8.1%). To compare the two exits fairly, each gain is turned into a **percentage of the exiting airline's share**.

### Formula
$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}} \times 100$$

In words: **the group's change ÷ the exiting airline's old share × 100.**
- $\Delta s_g$ = the group's change (Step 9)
- $\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}$ = the exiting airline's average share before (Step 8): 8.08 for Go First, 13.82 for Jet

### Example: Go First exit (passengers)

| Group | Working | $a_g$ |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 5.33 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **66.0%** |
| Akasa Air | 2.86 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **35.3%** |
| Air India Group | 2.72 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **33.7%** |
| Star Air | 0.15 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | 1.8% |
| Fly91, India One Air | | 0.2% |
| Flybig | −0.11 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | −1.3% |
| Alliance Air | −0.16 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | −2.0% |
| SpiceJet | −2.72 ÷ 8.08 × 100 | **−33.7%** |
| **Total** | | **100%** |

### How to read it

**1. The total is always 100%.**
Step 9 showed the changes add up to Go First's 8.08, so dividing each by 8.08 makes the ratios add up to 100%. That's the check written as $\sum_{g\neq x} a_g = 100\%$.

**2. A negative value means the group lost share.**
SpiceJet's −33.7% means that instead of taking any of Go First's share, SpiceJet *also* lost share. Its loss is roughly as big as the Air India Group's gain.

**3. The gainers together took more than 100%.**
IndiGo + Akasa + Air India Group = 66 + 35 + 34 = **135%**. They took all of Go First's share **plus** 35% more, which came from the shrinking airlines (SpiceJet, Alliance, Flybig).

### Comparing the two exits

| Group | After Jet (2019) | After Go First (2023) |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 37.7% | **66.0%** |
| SpiceJet | **22.9%** | −33.7% |
| Vistara | 14.3% | (inside Air India Group) |
| Go First | 14.1% | (exited) |
| AirAsia India | 10.6% | (inside Air India Group) |
| Air India Group | −1.0% | 33.7% |
| Akasa Air | (didn't exist) | 35.3% |

**What the comparison shows:**
- After Jet, the exiting share was **spread across five airlines**. The biggest single gainer, IndiGo, took about 38%.
- After Go First, it went **mostly to IndiGo** (66%), with the rest going to Akasa and the Air India Group.
- IndiGo's portion almost doubled. The hypothesis says IndiGo takes the largest portion, and more after Go First than after Jet, and this direction matches it (that's for Assignment 3 to confirm).

**Caveat from Step 8:** Akasa's 35% is mostly its own growth. It was already at 4% before Go First stopped flying. The absorption ratio measures *who gained in the same period*, not *who took Go First's actual passengers*. That difference belongs in the Assignment 3 limitations.

### What comes out of Step 10
`pct_of_exiting_share` in

. It is blank for the exiting airline itself.

That completes **Stage B**. Stage C (Steps 11–15) uses these numbers in the extra formulas.

## Step 11: Contribution to the rise in HHI

**The question it answers:** "Whose gain made the market more *concentrated*?"

$$c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2, \qquad \Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g$$

**Where it comes from:** HHI is the sum of squared shares. If a share moves from $s$ to $s+\Delta$, its square changes by $(s+\Delta)^2 - s^2 = 2s\Delta + \Delta^2$. The exiting airline's square simply disappears: $-(\bar s_x^{\text{pre}})^2$.

| Group | Go First exit | Points | Jet exit | Points |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Exiting airline | −(8.08)² | −65 | −(13.82)² | −191 |
| IndiGo | 2×56.6×5.33 + 5.33² | **+631** | 2×42.8×5.21 + 5.21² | **+473** |
| Air India Group | 2×24.6×2.72 + 2.72² | +141 | | −3 |
| Akasa | 2×1.6×2.86 + 2.86² | +18 | — | — |
| SpiceJet | 2×7.6×(−2.72) + 2.72² | −34 | 2×12.6×3.16 + 3.16² | +89 |
| Go First | (exited) | | | +39 |
| Vistara + AirAsia India | (in Air India Group) | | | +37 |
| **ΔHHI** | | **≈ +690** | | **≈ +444** |

**Key reading:** the $2\bar s^{\text{pre}}$ part means a gain is weighted by how big the firm already was.
- Akasa gained about as much share as the Air India Group but added only 18 points, against 141.
- IndiGo's gain alone is **more than the whole rise** after Jet (473 vs. 444), and **about 92%** of it after Go First.

## Step 12: Passengers vs. seat-km

**The question it answers:** "Did a group grow by filling seats or by adding planes?"

Run Step 10 again on seat-km and compare:

| Exit | Group | $a_g$ passengers | $a_g$ seat-km | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jet | **SpiceJet** | 22.9% | **30.4%** | **Capacity-led**: added planes |
| Jet | IndiGo | **37.7%** | 28.5% | Demand-led: filled existing seats |
| Jet | AirAsia India | 10.6% | 13.3% | Capacity-led |
| Go First | **Akasa** | 35.3% | **40.7%** | **Capacity-led** |
| Go First | Air India Group | **33.7%** | 30.3% | Demand-led |
| Go First | IndiGo | 66.0% | 66.0% | Both together |

**Why it matters:** SpiceJet's capacity-led gain after Jet matches its annual report: **31 aircraft inducted, 74 slots allotted**. Steps 10 and 12 give the *what*, and the filings give the *why*.

## Step 13: Mechanical merger ΔHHI

**The question it answers:** "How much does HHI jump *just because* brands now have one owner?"

$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a s_b$$

**Where it comes from:** $(s_a+s_b)^2 = s_a^2 + s_b^2 + 2s_as_b$. The extra $2s_as_b$ is the jump. Nobody switched airline; the shares are simply counted together.

**January 2022, Tata acquisition** (shares in December 2021):

| Brand | Share |
|---|---|
| Air India + AI Express | 8.46% |
| Vistara | 7.72% |
| AirAsia India | 6.28% |

$$2 \times (8.46 \times 7.72 + 8.46 \times 6.28 + 7.72 \times 6.28) = 2 \times 166.9 = \textbf{+334}$$

**December 2024 mergers** (brand shares in September 2024): Vistara merged into Air India, and AIX Connect into Air India Express:

$$2 \times (11.14 \times 10.04) + 2 \times (4.11 \times 3.97) = 224 + 33 = \textbf{+256}$$

## Step 14: Observed vs. mechanical

**The question it answers:** "Did the market concentrate *more* than the ownership change alone explains?"

| Event | Measure | Mechanical | Observed | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2022 acquisition | Ownership HHI | +334 | +373 | **+39** |
| Dec 2024 mergers | Brand HHI | +256 | +493 | **+237** |

**Reading:**
- In 2022, almost all of the jump is the ownership change itself.
- In 2024, about half is the brand merger. The other half is the market still moving: IndiGo kept growing and SpiceJet kept shrinking.

## Step 15: Fringe share

**The question it answers:** "Did the low-cost rivals CCI relied on stay strong?"

$$F_t = 100 - \text{CR2}_t$$

| Period | Mean fringe share |
|---|---|
| FY2022–23 (the data CCI looked at) | **19.2%** |
| After approval (Oct 2023 – Jul 2026) | **9.6%** |

**Reading:** the competition outside IndiGo and the Air India Group **halved** after CCI's approval.

## Step 11: Contribution to the rise in HHI

**The question it answers:** "Whose gain made the market more *concentrated*?"

$$c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2, \qquad \Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g$$

**Where it comes from:** HHI is the sum of squared shares. If a share moves from $s$ to $s+\Delta$, its square changes by $(s+\Delta)^2 - s^2 = 2s\Delta + \Delta^2$. The exiting airline's square simply disappears: $-(\bar s_x^{\text{pre}})^2$.

| Group | Go First exit | Points | Jet exit | Points |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Exiting airline | −(8.08)² | −65 | −(13.82)² | −191 |
| IndiGo | 2×56.6×5.33 + 5.33² | **+631** | 2×42.8×5.21 + 5.21² | **+473** |
| Air India Group | 2×24.6×2.72 + 2.72² | +141 | | −3 |
| Akasa | 2×1.6×2.86 + 2.86² | +18 | — | — |
| SpiceJet | 2×7.6×(−2.72) + 2.72² | −34 | 2×12.6×3.16 + 3.16² | +89 |
| Go First | (exited) | | | +39 |
| Vistara + AirAsia India | (in Air India Group) | | | +37 |
| **ΔHHI** | | **≈ +690** | | **≈ +444** |

**Key reading:** the $2\bar s^{\text{pre}}$ part means a gain is weighted by how big the firm already was.
- Akasa gained about as much share as the Air India Group but added only 18 points, against 141.
- IndiGo's gain alone is **more than the whole rise** after Jet (473 vs. 444), and **about 92%** of it after Go First.

children.text: \subsection{O2: Who gained from exits and consolidation}

$s_{gt}$ is the share of ownership group $g$ in month $t$, with $Q$ as passengers or seat-km. $\bar s_g^{\,k}$ is its mean over a window of up to 12 months before ($k=\text{pre}$) or after ($k=\text{post}$) an exit, excluding the exit month.
\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}, \qquad a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}} \times 100

$\Delta s_g$ is the change in share. $a_g$ is the portion of the exiting airline $x$'s share taken by $g$ (all $a_g$ sum to 100\%). A higher $a_g$ for seat-km than for passengers marks capacity-led growth, checked against company filings \parencite{spicejet2020annual,goair2021drhp}.
c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2, \qquad \Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g \neq x} c_g
$c_g$ is group $g$'s contribution to the change in \HHI{}. $\Delta\text{HHI}$ is the total change after the exit.

$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}}$ is the rise in \HHI{} from common ownership alone, for brands $G$ at pre-event shares. It is compared with the observed change in ownership \HHI{} at the January 2022 acquisition and in brand \HHI{} at the December 2024 mergers. $F_t$ is the fringe share, compared before and after CCI's approval to test its reliance on low-cost rivals \parencite{cci2023vistara}.

\textbf{Justification.} Two exits and two consolidation steps are too few for a regression. A before-and-after decomposition shows directly where the share went, the filings explain why, and the CCI order grounds the policy discussion in the regulator's actual reasoning.

## Final list of steps: raw data → clean data → O2 formulas

### Stage A: Raw data → clean data
**Input:**

(3,482 rows)

1. **Keep scheduled domestic only.** Drop international and non-scheduled (charter) rows.
2. **Drop rows with zero passengers.** That removes 132 rows: cargo airlines (Blue Dart, QuikJet), small airlines in months they weren't flying, and Jet Airways after its shutdown.
3. **Build a date.**

→ first of the month (e.g. 2023-06-01).
4. **Keep the needed columns.**

, `seat_km`, `passenger_km`, `plf`.
5. **Add ownership groups.**
   - Jet Airways + JetLite → Jet Airways Group
   - Air India + Air India Express → Air India Group
   - Vistara, AirAsia India, AIX Connect → Air India Group from January 2022
   - All others → own name

**Output:**

(1,577 rows, January 2015 – July 2026)

### Stage B: Clean data → exit decomposition
6. **Monthly shares**, for passengers and for seat-km:
$$s_{gt} = \frac{Q_{gt}}{\sum_j Q_{jt}} \times 100$$
7. **Set the windows** (exit month left out):
   - Jet: Apr 2018 – Mar 2019 vs. May 2019 – Feb 2020
   - Go First: May 2022 – Apr 2023 vs. Jun 2023 – May 2024
8. **Average share in each window:**
$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^k|}\sum_{t\in W^k} s_{gt}$$
9. **Change in share:**
$$\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$
10. **Absorption ratio:**
$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}} \times 100$$

**Output:**

edits.text:
# O2 pipeline: raw data → clean data → formulas

How the O2 numbers (who gained from exits and consolidation) are built, step by step, with a small real example for each step.

| Stage | What it does | Input → output |
|---|---|---|
| A | Clean the raw DGCA data | `data/raw/carrier_monthly.csv` → `data/processed/clean_scheduled_domestic.csv` |
| B | Exit decomposition | `clean_scheduled_domestic.csv` → `data/processed/exit_share_decomposition.csv` (script: `decompose_exits.py`) |
| C | Extra O2 calculations | Uses the Stage B output, `event_window_comparisons.csv` and the clean data. **Not yet saved in any file.** |

Examples use passenger shares and the **Go First exit (May 2023)** unless stated otherwise.

---

## Stage A: Raw data → clean data

Raw file: 3,482 rows (every airline, month and service type).

### Step 1: Keep scheduled domestic only
Keep rows where `service_type` = `scheduled_domestic`. International and non-scheduled (charter) rows are dropped.

> Example: an Air India row for international flights is dropped. Its domestic row for the same month is kept.

### Step 2: Drop rows with zero passengers
132 rows have 0 passengers:

| Reason | Airlines | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| Cargo-only airlines | Blue Dart Aviation, QuikJet Cargo | 111 |
| Small airlines in months they did not fly | Zoom Air, Air Pegasus, Air Odisha, Air Deccan | 17 |
| Listed just after shutting down | Jet Airways, JetLite (May–Jun 2019) | 4 |

> Example: Jet Airways, May 2019, 0 passengers → dropped.

### Step 3: Build a date
`year` + `month` → first day of that month.

> Example: year 2023, month 6 → `2023-06-01`.

### Step 4: Keep the needed columns
`date`, `airline`, `passengers`, `seat_km`, `passenger_km`, `plf`.

- **seat_km** = seats offered × km flown (capacity), in thousands
- **passenger_km** = passengers × km flown (capacity used), in thousands
- **plf** = passenger_km ÷ seat_km × 100 (how full the planes were)

> Example (one flight): 180 seats, 150 passengers, 1,150 km → seat-km 207,000, passenger-km 172,500, PLF 83.3%.

### Step 5: Add ownership groups

| Airlines | Group |
|---|---|
| Jet Airways + JetLite | Jet Airways Group (always) |
| Air India + Air India Express | Air India Group (always) |
| Vistara, AirAsia India, AIX Connect | Air India Group **from January 2022**, separate before |
| All others | Own name |

> Example: Vistara in June 2021 → "Vistara". Vistara in June 2023 → "Air India Group".

**Output:** `clean_scheduled_domestic.csv`, 1,577 rows, January 2015 – July 2026.

---

## Stage B: Clean data → exit decomposition

### Step 6: Monthly shares

$$s_{gt} = \frac{Q_{gt}}{\sum_j Q_{jt}} \times 100$$

Add up each group in a month, divide by the market total, × 100. Done twice: with passengers and with seat-km.

> Example, June 2023 (total 12,486,601 passengers):
>
> | Group | Passengers | Share |
> |---|---|---|
> | IndiGo | 7,893,296 | 63.2% |
> | Air India Group (Air India 1,212,719 + Vistara 1,011,426 + AirAsia India 1,003,619) | 3,227,764 | 25.9% |
> | Akasa Air | 618,053 | 4.9% |
> | SpiceJet | 555,248 | 4.4% |

### Step 7: Set the windows

| Exit | Before | Left out | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jet Airways (stopped 17 Apr 2019) | Apr 2018 – Mar 2019 | Apr 2019 | May 2019 – Feb 2020 (stops before COVID) |
| Go First (stopped 3 May 2023) | May 2022 – Apr 2023 | May 2023 | Jun 2023 – May 2024 |

> Why leave out the exit month: Go First flew only part of May 2023 (0.4% share), so that month is neither before nor after.
>
> Why Jet's window stops at Feb 2020: passengers fell from 12.3 m (Feb 2020) to 7.7 m (Mar 2020) to 0.3 m (May 2020) because of COVID.

### Step 8: Average share in each window

$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^k|}\sum_{t\in W^k} s_{gt}$$

Add the group's monthly shares in the window and divide by the number of months. Months before an airline existed count as 0%.

> Example, IndiGo: 12 monthly shares from 55.6 to 57.5 → **before 56.56%**. 12 monthly shares from 60.1 to 63.4 → **after 61.89%**.
>
> Example, Akasa: 0, 0, 0 (before it started flying), then 0.2 … 4.0 → **before 1.64%**. About 4.2–5.2 → **after 4.50%**.

### Step 9: Change in share

$$\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$

Reported in percentage points (pp). All changes add up to 0, because shares always total 100.

> | Group | Before | After | Change |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | IndiGo | 56.56 | 61.89 | +5.33 |
> | Akasa Air | 1.64 | 4.50 | +2.86 |
> | Air India Group | 24.55 | 27.27 | +2.72 |
> | SpiceJet | 7.64 | 4.91 | −2.72 |
> | Go First | 8.08 | 0 | −8.08 |

### Step 10: Absorption ratio

$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}} \times 100$$

The portion of the exiting airline's share each group took. The ratios add up to 100%, and a negative value means the group lost share.

> | Group | Working | $a_g$ |
> |---|---|---|
> | IndiGo | 5.33 ÷ 8.08 | 66.0% |
> | Akasa Air | 2.86 ÷ 8.08 | 35.3% |
> | Air India Group | 2.72 ÷ 8.08 | 33.7% |
> | SpiceJet | −2.72 ÷ 8.08 | −33.7% |
> | Others | | −1.3% |
> | **Total** | | **100%** |

**Output:** `exit_share_decomposition.csv` (columns `pre_share`, `post_share`, `change_pp`, `exiting_pre_share`, `pct_of_exiting_share`).

---

## Stage C: Extra O2 calculations

### Step 11: Contribution to the rise in HHI

$$c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2, \qquad \Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g$$

HHI is the sum of squared shares, so a share moving from $s$ to $s+\Delta$ changes HHI by $2s\Delta + \Delta^2$. A gain going to an already large group raises HHI more.

> | Part | Working | Points |
> |---|---|---|
> | Go First disappears | −(8.08)² | −65 |
> | IndiGo | 2 × 56.56 × 5.33 + 5.33² | +631 |
> | Air India Group | 2 × 24.55 × 2.72 + 2.72² | +141 |
> | Akasa Air | 2 × 1.64 × 2.86 + 2.86² | +18 |
> | SpiceJet | 2 × 7.64 × (−2.72) + 2.72² | −34 |
> | **Total ΔHHI** | | **≈ +690** |
>
> Akasa and the Air India Group gained similar share (+2.9 vs +2.7 pp) but added 18 vs 141 points. Jet exit total: ≈ +444, with IndiGo alone +473.

### Step 12: Passengers vs seat-km

Compare $a_g$ for passengers with $a_g$ for seat-km. A higher seat-km ratio means growth through added aircraft and flights (capacity-led), which is checked against company filings.

> | Exit | Group | $a_g$ passengers | $a_g$ seat-km | Reading |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Jet | SpiceJet | 22.9% | 30.4% | Capacity-led. Matches 74 slots and 31 aircraft in its FY2019-20 annual report (p. 62). |
> | Go First | Akasa Air | 35.3% | 40.7% | Capacity-led |
> | Go First | Air India Group | 33.7% | 30.3% | Demand-led (filled existing seats) |

### Step 13: Mechanical merger ΔHHI

$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a s_b$$

When brands get one owner nobody switches airline, but HHI jumps because $(s_a+s_b)^2 = s_a^2 + s_b^2 + 2s_as_b$.

> **Jan 2022 acquisition** (Dec 2021 shares: Air India + AI Express 8.46, Vistara 7.72, AirAsia India 6.28):
> 2 × (8.46 × 7.72 + 8.46 × 6.28 + 7.72 × 6.28) ≈ **+334**
>
> **Dec 2024 mergers** (Sep 2024 shares: Air India 11.14 + Vistara 10.04; AI Express 3.97 + AIX Connect 4.11):
> 2 × (11.14 × 10.04) + 2 × (3.97 × 4.11) ≈ **+256**

### Step 14: Observed vs mechanical

Compare Step 13 with the observed 12-month window change in `event_window_comparisons.csv`. Use **ownership HHI for Jan 2022** and **brand HHI for Dec 2024**, because ownership HHI already groups the Tata brands from Jan 2022 (so its mechanical jump in Dec 2024 is 0). The result is discussed against CCI's combination order.

> | Event | Measure | Mechanical | Observed | Difference |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Jan 2022 | Ownership HHI | +334 | +373 | +39 |
> | Dec 2024 | Brand HHI | +256 | +493 | +237 |

### Deferred: fringe-share test of CCI's assumption
Removed from O2 for now (overlaps O4). Fringe share = 100 − CR2: about 19.2% in FY2022–23 vs 9.6% after Sept 2023. Revisit once O4 is done.

---

## Mapping to the paper (Assignment 2, §5.2)

| Paper | Steps |
|---|---|
| A. Exits, Stage 1: Market shares | 6–8 |
| A. Exits, Stage 2: Who absorbed the exiting share | 9–10, 12 |
| A. Exits, Stage 3: Who drove concentration | 11 |
| B. Consolidation, Stage 1: Effect of common ownership | 13–14 |

Stage A (Steps 1–5) is data preparation, covered in Sections 2–3 and the data appendix.

## Caveats for Assignment 3

- **Own trends:** Akasa was already at 4.0% in Apr 2023, before Go First stopped, so much of its +2.86 pp is its own growth. Jet was already falling before its exit (11.4% Feb 2019 → 5.7% Mar 2019).
- **Small differences:** Step 11 uses the HHI of window-average shares (Go First ≈ 690). `event_window_comparisons.csv` averages the monthly HHIs (686). Both are correct, just computed differently.
- **Not yet in code:** Steps 11–14 were calculated by hand. Add them to `decompose_exits.py` for reproducibility.
