| Air India + Air India Express | Air India Group (always) |
| Vistara, AirAsia India, AIX Connect | Air India Group **from January 2022**, separate before |
| All others | Own name |

> Example: Vistara in June 2021 → "Vistara". Vistara in June 2023 → "Air India Group".

**Output:** `clean_scheduled_domestic.csv`, 1,577 rows, January 2015 – July 2026.

---

## Stage B: Clean data → exit decomposition

### Step 6: Monthly shares

$$s_{gt} = \frac{Q_{gt}}{\sum_j Q_{jt}} \times 100$$

Add up each group in a month, divide by the market total, × 100. Done twice: with passengers and with seat-km.

> Example, June 2023 (total 12,486,601 passengers):
>
> | Group | Passengers | Share |
> |---|---|---|
> | IndiGo | 7,893,296 | 63.2% |
> | Air India Group (Air India 1,212,719 + Vistara 1,011,426 + AirAsia India 1,003,619) | 3,227,764 | 25.9% |
> | Akasa Air | 618,053 | 4.9% |
> | SpiceJet | 555,248 | 4.4% |

### Step 7: Set the windows

| Exit | Before | Left out | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jet Airways (stopped 17 Apr 2019) | Apr 2018 – Mar 2019 | Apr 2019 | May 2019 – Feb 2020 (stops before COVID) |
| Go First (stopped 3 May 2023) | May 2022 – Apr 2023 | May 2023 | Jun 2023 – May 2024 |

> Why leave out the exit month: Go First flew only part of May 2023 (0.4% share), so that month is neither before nor after.
>
> Why Jet's window stops at Feb 2020: passengers fell from 12.3 m (Feb 2020) to 7.7 m (Mar 2020) to 0.3 m (May 2020) because of COVID.

### Step 8: Average share in each window

$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^k|}\sum_{t\in W^k} s_{gt}$$

Add the group's monthly shares in the window and divide by the number of months. Months before an airline existed count as 0%.

> Example, IndiGo: 12 monthly shares from 55.6 to 57.5 → **before 56.56%**. 12 monthly shares from 60.1 to 63.4 → **after 61.89%**.
>
> Example, Akasa: 0, 0, 0 (before it started flying), then 0.2 … 4.0 → **before 1.64%**. About 4.2–5.2 → **after 4.50%**.

### Step 9: Change in share

$$\Delta s_g = \bar s_g^{\,\text{post}} - \bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}$$

Reported in percentage points (pp). All changes add up to 0, because shares always total 100.

> | Group | Before | After | Change |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | IndiGo | 56.56 | 61.89 | +5.33 |
> | Akasa Air | 1.64 | 4.50 | +2.86 |
> | Air India Group | 24.55 | 27.27 | +2.72 |
> | SpiceJet | 7.64 | 4.91 | −2.72 |
> | Go First | 8.08 | 0 | −8.08 |

### Step 10: Absorption ratio

$$a_g = \frac{\Delta s_g}{\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}} \times 100$$

The portion of the exiting airline's share each group took. The ratios add up to 100%, and a negative value means the group lost share.

> | Group | Working | $a_g$ |
> |---|---|---|
> | IndiGo | 5.33 ÷ 8.08 | 66.0% |
> | Akasa Air | 2.86 ÷ 8.08 | 35.3% |
> | Air India Group | 2.72 ÷ 8.08 | 33.7% |
> | SpiceJet | −2.72 ÷ 8.08 | −33.7% |
> | Others | | −1.3% |
> | **Total** | | **100%** |

**Output:** `exit_share_decomposition.csv` (columns `pre_share`, `post_share`, `change_pp`, `exiting_pre_share`, `pct_of_exiting_share`).

---

## Stage C: Extra O2 calculations

### Step 11: Contribution to the rise in HHI

$$c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2, \qquad \Delta\text{HHI} = -\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 + \sum_{g\neq x} c_g$$

HHI is the sum of squared shares, so a share moving from $s$ to $s+\Delta$ changes HHI by $2s\Delta + \Delta^2$. A gain going to an already large group raises HHI more.

> | Part | Working | Points |
> |---|---|---|
> | Go First disappears | −(8.08)² | −65 |
> | IndiGo | 2 × 56.56 × 5.33 + 5.33² | +631 |
> | Air India Group | 2 × 24.55 × 2.72 + 2.72² | +141 |
> | Akasa Air | 2 × 1.64 × 2.86 + 2.86² | +18 |
> | SpiceJet | 2 × 7.64 × (−2.72) + 2.72² | −34 |
> | **Total ΔHHI** | | **≈ +690** |
>
> Akasa and the Air India Group gained similar share (+2.9 vs +2.7 pp) but added 18 vs 141 points. Jet exit total: ≈ +444, with IndiGo alone +473.

### Step 12: Passengers vs seat-km

Compare $a_g$ for passengers with $a_g$ for seat-km. A higher seat-km ratio means growth through added aircraft and flights (capacity-led), which is checked against company filings.

> | Exit | Group | $a_g$ passengers | $a_g$ seat-km | Reading |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Jet | SpiceJet | 22.9% | 30.4% | Capacity-led. Matches 74 slots and 31 aircraft in its FY2019-20 annual report (p. 62). |
> | Go First | Akasa Air | 35.3% | 40.7% | Capacity-led |
> | Go First | Air India Group | 33.7% | 30.3% | Demand-led (filled existing seats) |

### Step 13: Mechanical merger ΔHHI

$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a s_b$$

When brands get one owner nobody switches airline, but HHI jumps because $(s_a+s_b)^2 = s_a^2 + s_b^2 + 2s_as_b$.

> **Jan 2022 acquisition** (Dec 2021 shares: Air India + AI Express 8.46, Vistara 7.72, AirAsia India 6.28):
> 2 × (8.46 × 7.72 + 8.46 × 6.28 + 7.72 × 6.28) ≈ **+334**
>
> **Dec 2024 mergers** (Sep 2024 shares: Air India 11.14 + Vistara 10.04; AI Express 3.97 + AIX Connect 4.11):
> 2 × (11.14 × 10.04) + 2 × (3.97 × 4.11) ≈ **+256**

### Step 14: Observed vs mechanical

Compare Step 13 with the observed 12-month window change in `event_window_comparisons.csv`. Use **ownership HHI for Jan 2022** and **brand HHI for Dec 2024**, because ownership HHI already groups the Tata brands from Jan 2022 (so its mechanical jump in Dec 2024 is 0). The result is discussed against CCI's combination order.

> | Event | Measure | Mechanical | Observed | Difference |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Jan 2022 | Ownership HHI | +334 | +373 | +39 |
> | Dec 2024 | Brand HHI | +256 | +493 | +237 |

### Deferred: fringe-share test of CCI's assumption
Removed from O2 for now (overlaps O4). Fringe share = 100 − CR2: about 19.2% in FY2022–23 vs 9.6% after Sept 2023. Revisit once O4 is done.

---

## Mapping to the paper (Assignment 2, §5.2)

| Paper | Steps |
|---|---|
| A. Exits, Stage 1: Market shares | 6–8 |
| A. Exits, Stage 2: Who absorbed the exiting share | 9–10, 12 |
| A. Exits, Stage 3: Who drove concentration | 11 |
| B. Consolidation, Stage 1: Effect of common ownership | 13–14 |

Stage A (Steps 1–5) is data preparation, covered in Sections 2–3 and the data appendix.

## Caveats for Assignment 3

- **Own trends:** Akasa was already at 4.0% in Apr 2023, before Go First stopped, so much of its +2.86 pp is its own growth. Jet was already falling before its exit (11.4% Feb 2019 → 5.7% Mar 2019).
- **Small differences:** Step 11 uses the HHI of window-average shares (Go First ≈ 690). `event_window_comparisons.csv` averages the monthly HHIs (686). Both are correct, just computed differently.
- **Not yet in code:** Steps 11–14 were calculated by hand. Add them to `decompose_exits.py` for reproducibility.
"}

response.value:
## 1. What "concentration" means

**Concentration = how much of the market is held by a few firms.**

Two simple markets, each with 100 passengers:

| Market X | Share | Market Y | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Airline A | 25% | Airline A | 70% |
| Airline B | 25% | Airline B | 10% |
| Airline C | 25% | Airline C | 10% |
| Airline D | 25% | Airline D | 10% |

- **Market X** is **not concentrated**: four equal players, and passengers have real choices.
- **Market Y** is **highly concentrated**: one airline dominates.

**HHI** turns this into a single number: square each share and add them up.
- Market X: 25² + 25² + 25² + 25² = **2,500**
- Market Y: 70² + 10² + 10² + 10² = **5,200**

**Higher HHI means more concentrated** (up to 10,000 for a monopoly). Indian aviation today is about **5,000**.

## 2. What "concentration rose from common ownership alone" means

Start with three airlines, each with a third of the market:

| Airline | Owner | Share |
|---|---|---|
| A | Owner 1 | 33% |
| B | Owner 2 | 33% |
| C | Owner 3 | 33% |

HHI = 33² + 33² + 33² ≈ **3,300**

**Now Owner 1 buys Airline B.** Nothing else changes:
- No passenger switches airline.
- No flight changes.
- A and B still fly under their own names.

But A and B now have **one owner**, who decides prices and routes for both. Economically, there are now **two** independent competitors, not three:

| Owner | Airlines | Combined share |
|---|---|---|
| Owner 1 | A + B | 66% |
| Owner 3 | C | 33% |

HHI = 66² + 33² ≈ **5,450**

**HHI rose by about 2,150, yet not a single passenger moved.** That's the rise from common ownership alone: it comes purely from *who owns* the airlines, not from passengers moving.

### The formula behind it
When A (share $s_A$) and B (share $s_B$) get one owner:
- Before: $s_A^2 + s_B^2$
- After: $(s_A + s_B)^2 = s_A^2 + s_B^2 + \mathbf{2 s_A s_B}$

The extra part, $2 s_A s_B$, is the jump. In the example: 2 × 33 × 33 ≈ 2,178.

## 3. The real Tata case

In December 2021 these were separate firms:

| Airline | Share |
|---|---|
| Air India (+ AI Express) | 8.5% |
| Vistara | 7.7% |
| AirAsia India | 6.3% |

In **January 2022** Tata took over Air India and treated all three as one group. The next day, nobody had switched airline, but the group was now one competitor with about 22.5% instead of three smaller ones.

Mechanical jump = 2 × (8.5 × 7.7 + 8.5 × 6.3 + 7.7 × 6.3) ≈ **+334 HHI points**

## 4. Why this matters for your objective

| | **Exits** (Part A) | **Mergers** (Part B) |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | An airline disappears | Airlines get one owner |
| Do passengers move? | **Yes**, to other airlines | **No**, nobody switches |
| Why concentration rises | Passengers go mostly to big airlines | Shares are now counted together |
| What you measure | Who took the passengers | How much HHI rose from ownership alone (+334) |

**Then you compare:** the actual rise after January 2022 was **+373**. About 334 of that came from common ownership. The other ~39 came from the market itself changing afterwards.

**In one sentence:** *"Even though no passenger switched airline, putting Air India, Vistara and AirAsia India under one owner raised concentration by about 334 points, because three competitors became one."*

toolCallRounds.response:
## 1. What "concentration" means

**Concentration = how much of the market is held by a few firms.**

Two simple markets, each with 100 passengers:

| Market X | Share | Market Y | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Airline A | 25% | Airline A | 70% |
| Airline B | 25% | Airline B | 10% |
| Airline C | 25% | Airline C | 10% |
| Airline D | 25% | Airline D | 10% |

- **Market X** is **not concentrated**: four equal players, and passengers have real choices.
- **Market Y** is **highly concentrated**: one airline dominates.

**HHI** turns this into a single number: square each share and add them up.
- Market X: 25² + 25² + 25² + 25² = **2,500**
- Market Y: 70² + 10² + 10² + 10² = **5,200**

**Higher HHI means more concentrated** (up to 10,000 for a monopoly). Indian aviation today is about **5,000**.

## 2. What "concentration rose from common ownership alone" means

Start with three airlines, each with a third of the market:

| Airline | Owner | Share |
|---|---|---|
| A | Owner 1 | 33% |
| B | Owner 2 | 33% |
| C | Owner 3 | 33% |

HHI = 33² + 33² + 33² ≈ **3,300**

**Now Owner 1 buys Airline B.** Nothing else changes:
- No passenger switches airline.
- No flight changes.
- A and B still fly under their own names.

But A and B now have **one owner**, who decides prices and routes for both. Economically, there are now **two** independent competitors, not three:

| Owner | Airlines | Combined share |
|---|---|---|
| Owner 1 | A + B | 66% |
| Owner 3 | C | 33% |

HHI = 66² + 33² ≈ **5,450**

**HHI rose by about 2,150, yet not a single passenger moved.** That's the rise from common ownership alone: it comes purely from *who owns* the airlines, not from passengers moving.

### The formula behind it
When A (share $s_A$) and B (share $s_B$) get one owner:
- Before: $s_A^2 + s_B^2$
- After: $(s_A + s_B)^2 = s_A^2 + s_B^2 + \mathbf{2 s_A s_B}$

The extra part, $2 s_A s_B$, is the jump. In the example: 2 × 33 × 33 ≈ 2,178.

## 3. The real Tata case

In December 2021 these were separate firms:

| Airline | Share |
|---|---|
| Air India (+ AI Express) | 8.5% |
| Vistara | 7.7% |
| AirAsia India | 6.3% |

In **January 2022** Tata took over Air India and treated all three as one group. The next day, nobody had switched airline, but the group was now one competitor with about 22.5% instead of three smaller ones.

Mechanical jump = 2 × (8.5 × 7.7 + 8.5 × 6.3 + 7.7 × 6.3) ≈ **+334 HHI points**

## 4. Why this matters for your objective

| | **Exits** (Part A) | **Mergers** (Part B) |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | An airline disappears | Airlines get one owner |
| Do passengers move? | **Yes**, to other airlines | **No**, nobody switches |
| Why concentration rises | Passengers go mostly to big airlines | Shares are now counted together |
| What you measure | Who took the passengers | How much HHI rose from ownership alone (+334) |

**Then you compare:** the actual rise after January 2022 was **+373**. About 334 of that came from common ownership. The other ~39 came from the market itself changing afterwards.

**In one sentence:** *"Even though no passenger switched airline, putting Air India, Vistara and AirAsia India under one owner raised concentration by about 334 points, because three competitors became one."*

Three airlines join: **Air India (8.5)**, **Vistara (7.7)** and **AirAsia India (6.3)**. The formula $2\sum_{a<b} s_a s_b$ means: **take every pair of merging airlines, multiply their shares, add the results, then double.**

With three airlines there are three pairs:

| Pair | Multiply | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Air India × Vistara | 8.5 × 7.7 | 65.45 |
| Air India × AirAsia India | 8.5 × 6.3 | 53.55 |
| Vistara × AirAsia India | 7.7 × 6.3 | 48.51 |
| **Sum** | | **167.51** |

### Step 2: Double it
2 × 167.51 = **335**

(The 334 I gave earlier used unrounded shares: 8.46, 7.72, 6.28. Rounding to one decimal gives 335. Same answer.)

You can get the same number directly from the definition of HHI: compare the squared shares *before* and *after* they are counted together.

**Before** (three separate firms, each squared):
8.5² + 7.7² + 6.3² = 72.25 + 59.29 + 39.69 = **171.23**

**After** (one firm with the combined share, squared):
(8.5 + 7.7 + 6.3)² = 22.5² = **506.25**

**Jump:** 506.25 − 171.23 = **335** ✓

All other airlines (IndiGo, SpiceJet, …) keep the same shares, so their squares don't change and they drop out of the difference.

Squaring a sum gives the individual squares **plus every pair twice**:

Yes, you've got the measuring part. The technical name for "combining ownership" is **consolidation** (or a merger, or bringing airlines under **common ownership**). The +334 is called the **mechanical** or **merger-induced ΔHHI**.

Your objective asks for two things about the Tata consolidation:

| | What it means | Type |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Measure** | How much did concentration rise just from putting the airlines under one owner? (+334) | Numbers |
| **2. Discuss competition-policy implications** | What does that rise mean for the **regulator and passengers**, and did the regulator handle it well? | Interpretation |

## What "competition policy" means
**Competition policy** is the set of government rules that keep markets competitive, such as blocking harmful mergers or punishing firms that abuse their dominance. In India, the body that applies these rules is the **CCI (Competition Commission of India)**.

**"Competition-policy implications"** = *what our findings mean for those rules and that regulator.*

## What "using CCI's combination order as the primary source" means
Before the Air India–Vistara merger could happen, CCI had to approve it. Its decision (the **combination order**, September 2023) records:
- what CCI checked: **48 routes** where both airlines flew;
- what it worried about: a high combined share on some of those routes;
- why it still approved: it expected low-cost rivals and other airlines' slots to keep competition alive;
- the conditions it set: Air India must keep minimum capacity on **7 routes**.

**"Primary source"** = quote CCI's own document, not news reports about it.

## How the two parts connect
You **put your numbers next to CCI's reasoning** and ask what that shows:

| CCI said (2023) | Your data shows | Policy implication |
|---|---|---|

| Merger was fine because **low-cost rivals** would compete | Go First had already stopped flying before the approval; SpiceJet was shrinking | The competition CCI relied on was already weakening |
| Set conditions on **7 routes** | Air India Group is now about 25%, IndiGo about 64% | Conditions on a few routes may not address an overall duopoly |

- **Assignment 2 (now):** only the plan, i.e. "we will measure the mechanical ΔHHI and discuss it against CCI's combination order." That's done.
- **Assignment 3 (later):** the actual numbers and the discussion in the table above, ending with 2–3 policy recommendations (for example, "CCI should also look at ownership-adjusted national HHI, not only route overlaps").

**In one sentence:** *"We measure how much the Tata consolidation raised concentration from ownership alone, then use CCI's own approval order to discuss whether the regulator's route-level review and assumptions were enough, and what that means for competition policy."*

Yes, that's the idea. Keep three things in mind so the discussion is fair and accurate.

### 1. Treat it as a question, not a verdict
Ask *"Did CCI's reasons hold up?"*, not *"CCI was wrong."* Assignment 3 then answers with evidence, and either answer is fine. The guidelines say a well-argued result scores well even if it's not the one you expected.

### 3. Give CCI's side too
For a balanced discussion, also say why CCI's decision could be reasonable:
- CCI legally judges mergers **route by route**, and on most of the 48 routes it found enough competition.
- It didn't just say OK: it set **conditions** on the **7 routes** where it was worried.
- Your study measures **market structure only**, with no fare data (feedback #7). So you can say *competition weakened*, but not *passengers were harmed*.

### Your Part B discussion in one line
> *"CCI approved the merger because it expected other airlines to keep competing, but within months Go First had exited and SpiceJet was shrinking, so the competition it relied on was weaker than assumed. We discuss whether a route-level review with conditions on seven routes was enough, given how concentrated the national market became."*

response.value:
Here's the same idea with real data from **June 2023**.

## Level 1: Airline-month (supporting unit)
**One row = one airline in one month.** This is what's in

.

| date | airline | ownership_group | passengers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023-06 | IndiGo | IndiGo | 7,893,296 |
| 2023-06 | Air India | Air India Group | 1,212,719 |
| 2023-06 | Vistara | Air India Group | 1,011,426 |
| 2023-06 | AirAsia India | Air India Group | 1,003,619 |
| 2023-06 | Akasa Air | Akasa Air | 618,053 |
| 2023-06 | SpiceJet | SpiceJet | 555,248 |
| 2023-06 | Alliance Air | Alliance Air | 144,033 |
| 2023-06 | Star Air | Star Air | 24,554 |
| 2023-06 | Flybig | Flybig | 22,277 |
| 2023-06 | India One Air | India One Air | 1,376 |

That's **10 rows for June 2023**: one per airline.

## Middle step: Group by owner and calculate shares
Airlines with the same owner are added together, then each group is divided by the market total (12,486,601):

| ownership_group | passengers | share | share² |
|---|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 7,893,296 | 63.21% | 3,996 |
| Air India Group (3 airlines added) | 3,227,764 | 25.85% | 668 |
| Akasa Air | 618,053 | 4.95% | 25 |
| SpiceJet | 555,248 | 4.45% | 20 |
| Alliance Air | 144,033 | 1.15% | 1 |
| Others | 48,207 | 0.39% | ~0 |
| **Total** | **12,486,601** | **100%** | **4,710** |

## Level 2: Market-month (main unit)
**One row = the whole market in one month.** All 10 airline rows collapse into a single row. This is what's in

.

| date | total_passengers | ownership_hhi | ownership_cr2 | brand_hhi |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023-06 | 12,486,601 | **4,710** | **89.1%** | 4,266 |

- **ownership_hhi** = sum of squared group shares (the 4,710 above)
- **ownership_cr2** = top two groups: 63.21 + 25.85 = 89.1%
- **brand_hhi** = the same calculation with each airline counted separately (without grouping Air India, Vistara and AirAsia India)

## The picture
```
Airline-month (10 rows for June 2023)
   IndiGo | Air India | Vistara | AirAsia India | Akasa | SpiceJet | ...
        │            └───────┬──────────┘
        │              grouped by owner
        ▼                    ▼
   shares: IndiGo 63.2%, Air India Group 25.9%, ...
        │
        ▼  square and add
Market-month (1 row for June 2023)
   HHI = 4,710   CR2 = 89.1%
```

**In plain words:**
- **Airline-month** = "How many passengers did *each airline* carry in June 2023?"
- **Market-month** = "How concentrated was *the whole market* in June 2023?"

The market-month is the **main** unit because the research question is about **market concentration**. It is **built from** the airline-month rows, which is why the airline-month is called the **supporting** unit. Do this for all 138 months and you get 138 market-month rows: one HHI per month, January 2015 to July 2026.

## Your O2 unit has two halves

> **Ownership group before vs. after each exit** → **Part A (Exits)**
> **Market-month before vs. after each Tata consolidation step** → **Part B (Consolidation)**

## Part A: "Ownership group before vs. after each exit"

**Question:** *Who* took the exiting airline's share?

To answer "who", you need one number **per group**. So the unit is:
> **one ownership group, in one window (before or after), around one exit**

**Example (Go First exit), from

:**

| Exit | Group | Before (May 22 – Apr 23) | After (Jun 23 – May 24) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Go First | IndiGo | 56.56% | 61.89% |
| Go First | Air India Group | 24.55% | 27.27% |
| Go First | Akasa Air | 1.64% | 4.50% |
| Go First | SpiceJet | 7.64% | 4.91% |

Each row is a **group**, and each group has a **before** value and an **after** value. Each value is the average of 12 monthly shares.

## Part B: "Market-month before vs. after each Tata consolidation step"

**Question:** *How much* did concentration rise?

To answer "how much", you need one number for the **whole market**, which is HHI. HHI is calculated per month, so the unit is:
> **the whole market in one month, averaged over the months before and after each Tata step**

**Example (Tata acquisition, January 2022), from

:**

| Step | Measure | Before (Jan – Dec 2021) | After (Jan – Dec 2022) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2022 acquisition | Ownership HHI | 3,513 | 3,886 | **+373** |
| Dec 2024 mergers | Brand HHI | 4,066 | 4,559 | **+493** |

There's **one row per step**, with no breakdown by airline, because HHI describes the market as a whole. You then compare these observed changes with the mechanical jump (+334 and +256).

## Side by side

| | **Part A: Exits** | **Part B: Consolidation** |
|---|---|---|
| Question | *Who* gained? | *How much* did concentration rise? |
| One observation is | One **group** in one window | The whole **market** in one month |
| What's measured | Each group's share | Market HHI |
| Before / after | 12 months either side of the exit | 12 months either side of the Tata step |
| Example | IndiGo: 56.6% → 61.9% | Ownership HHI: 3,513 → 3,886 |

**Both come from the same airline-month data.** Part A groups it by owner and keeps the groups separate. Part B squares and adds the group shares into one HHI per month.

**In one line:** *"For exits I look at each ownership group's share before and after, to see who gained. For consolidation I look at the whole market's HHI before and after each Tata step, to see how much concentration rose."*

## Your O2 unit has two halves

> **Ownership group before vs. after each exit** → **Part A (Exits)**
> **Market-month before vs. after each Tata consolidation step** → **Part B (Consolidation)**

## Part A: "Ownership group before vs. after each exit"

**Question:** *Who* took the exiting airline's share?

To answer "who", you need one number **per group**. So the unit is:
> **one ownership group, in one window (before or after), around one exit**

**Example (Go First exit), from [exit_share_decomposition.csv](term-paper/analysis/data/processed/exit_share_decomposition.csv):**

| Exit | Group | Before (May 22 – Apr 23) | After (Jun 23 – May 24) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Go First | IndiGo | 56.56% | 61.89% |
| Go First | Air India Group | 24.55% | 27.27% |
| Go First | Akasa Air | 1.64% | 4.50% |
| Go First | SpiceJet | 7.64% | 4.91% |

Each row is a **group**, and each group has a **before** value and an **after** value. Each value is the average of 12 monthly shares.

## Part B: "Market-month before vs. after each Tata consolidation step"

**Question:** *How much* did concentration rise?

To answer "how much", you need one number for the **whole market**, which is HHI. HHI is calculated per month, so the unit is:
> **the whole market in one month, averaged over the months before and after each Tata step**

**Example (Tata acquisition, January 2022), from [event_window_comparisons.csv](term-paper/analysis/data/processed/event_window_comparisons.csv):**

| Step | Measure | Before (Jan – Dec 2021) | After (Jan – Dec 2022) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2022 acquisition | Ownership HHI | 3,513 | 3,886 | **+373** |
| Dec 2024 mergers | Brand HHI | 4,066 | 4,559 | **+493** |

There's **one row per step**, with no breakdown by airline, because HHI describes the market as a whole. You then compare these observed changes with the mechanical jump (+334 and +256).

## Side by side

| | **Part A: Exits** | **Part B: Consolidation** |
|---|---|---|
| Question | *Who* gained? | *How much* did concentration rise? |
| One observation is | One **group** in one window | The whole **market** in one month |
| What's measured | Each group's share | Market HHI |
| Before / after | 12 months either side of the exit | 12 months either side of the Tata step |
| Example | IndiGo: 56.6% → 61.9% | Ownership HHI: 3,513 → 3,886 |

**Both come from the same airline-month data.** Part A groups it by owner and keeps the groups separate. Part B squares and adds the group shares into one HHI per month.

**In one line:** *"For exits I look at each ownership group's share before and after, to see who gained. For consolidation I look at the whole market's HHI before and after each Tata step, to see how much concentration rose."*

## 1. DGCA monthly traffic data (the numbers for Parts A and B)
Shared with the team (gray), but your calculations all come from it.

| Column | What it says | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | DGCA monthly airline traffic, cleaned version (Kubicek, GitHub) | The government's official monthly figures for each airline, tidied into one CSV |

## 2. Company filings (Part A: slot and fleet evidence)

| Column | What it says | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | SpiceJet Annual Report 2019–20, Go Airlines DRHP 2021 | Documents the airlines themselves published. A DRHP (draft red herring prospectus) is the document a company files before listing on the stock market. |
| **Access** | Downloaded PDFs, pages recorded | Saved in `analysis/sources/`, with exact page numbers noted |
| **Used for** | O2 (feedback #5) | To explain **why** certain airlines could take the exiting share |

**What each filing tells you:**
- **SpiceJet (p. 62):** after a full-service carrier (Jet) stopped flying, SpiceJet was **allotted 74 slots** and **inducted 31 aircraft**. That's direct evidence it got Jet's slots and planes.
- **Go Airlines DRHP (p. 35):** Go First had **engine problems** (Pratt & Whitney) that grounded part of its fleet. That's evidence of why it was weakening before it exited.

**Limitations, line by line:**
| Limitation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| "Self-reported" | The airlines wrote these themselves, so they may present things favourably |
| "The Go Airlines prospectus pre-dates the 2023 exit" | It was filed in **2021**, two years before Go First stopped. It shows the engine trouble building up, but not the exit itself or who got its slots afterwards. |
| "SpiceJet's slot passage refers to 'a full service carrier' without naming Jet Airways" | The report never says "Jet Airways" in that sentence. We infer it's Jet from the timing (2019) and from another page that mentions Jet's closure. |

| Column | What it says | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | CCI combination order on Air India–Vistara | The regulator's own approval document (September 2023) |
| **Access** | Downloaded PDF (scanned), paragraphs recorded | It's a scanned image, so its text can't be searched or copied. Key paragraphs are noted in

. |
| **Used for** | O2 (feedback #6) | Primary source for the competition-policy discussion in Part B |

**Limitations, line by line:**
| Limitation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| "CCI defines the market as city pairs (48 overlapping domestic routes), not the national market we measure" | CCI checked **individual routes** (e.g. Delhi–Mumbai) where both airlines flew; there were 48. We measure the **whole national market**. So our numbers and CCI's aren't directly comparable: they look at the same merger from different levels. |
| "Share triggers in the commitments are redacted" | CCI set conditions on 7 routes (keep minimum capacity, etc.), but the **exact share levels** that would trigger action are **blacked out** in the public version. We know there are conditions, but not their exact thresholds. |

## How they fit together
```
DGCA data ──► Part A numbers (who gained)  ──► Company filings explain WHY
          └─► Part B numbers (HHI jump)    ──► CCI order: what the regulator said
```

response.value:
I'm noticing the bulleted rows have extra blank space pushing the whole row down, likely caused by a leading \par inside the first bullet cell creating unwanted vertical space before the content.

I think the fix is to avoid the leading `\par` before the first bullet — instead check if already in horizontal mode before inserting one, so the color whatsit doesn't create a stray empty first line that throws off vertical alignment in the p-column. The real culprit may be that `\color` in vertical mode inserts a whatsit into the vbox, shifting the baseline used for top-alignment relative to the other cells.

Other mine cells worked fine, so the color whatsit isn't actually the culprit—it must be something about \par interacting with the array package's p-column internals, like \@startpbox and how it inserts a strut at the start of the cell for correct first-line height.

If that strut opens horizontal mode before my \par, then \par would end the paragraph immediately, leaving an empty first line with just the strut—explaining the extra blank line before the bullet. But this doesn't fully match the image, since "Company filings:" and the bullet appear on the same visual line, both with a gap above, not one above the other.

So I should avoid issuing \par for the first bullet in each cell, only inserting it between subsequent bullets—maybe by defining separate first/non-first bullet macros, or simply placing \par manually between items in the source rather than baking it into the macro.

Bullets now render, but each cell has a blank line at the top since the macro inserts a break before the first bullet. I'll adjust it so the break only appears between bullets, not before the first one.

response.value:
You have five variables in the table (all in black). Here's each one with real values. A note on the units first:
- **pp** (percentage points): the difference between two percentages, e.g. 56% → 61% = +5 pp
- **%**: a portion of something, here the exiting airline's share
- **points**: HHI units, on a scale from 0 to 10,000

## 1. Change in share, $\Delta s_g$ (unit: pp)
**Definition:** mean share after an exit minus mean share before, for each group, using passengers and seat-km.
**In plain words:** how much bigger or smaller did each airline group get after the exit?

| Exit | Group | Before | After | $\Delta s_g$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go First | IndiGo | 56.56% | 61.89% | **+5.33 pp** |
| Go First | SpiceJet | 7.64% | 4.91% | **−2.72 pp** |
| Jet | SpiceJet | 12.58% | 15.74% | **+3.16 pp** |

Positive means the group gained, negative means it lost.

## 2. Absorption ratio, $a_g$ (unit: %)
**Definition:** $\Delta s_g$ divided by the exiting airline's mean share before the exit.
**In plain words:** what portion of the exiting airline's share did this group take?

| Exit | Exiting share | Group | $\Delta s_g$ | $a_g$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go First | 8.08% | IndiGo | +5.33 | 5.33 ÷ 8.08 = **66%** |
| Go First | 8.08% | SpiceJet | −2.72 | −2.72 ÷ 8.08 = **−34%** |
| Jet | 13.82% | IndiGo | +5.21 | 5.21 ÷ 13.82 = **38%** |

All groups together add up to 100%. This lets you compare exits of different sizes: IndiGo took 38% of Jet's share but 66% of Go First's.

## 3. Contribution to ΔHHI, $c_g$ (unit: points)
**Definition:** $2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2$
**In plain words:** how much of the rise in concentration was caused by *this* group's gain?

response.value:
I think I see the user's confusion—they may worry that dividing by 8 assumes everyone could take the whole amount or an equal share. But really, dividing by 8 just measures what was actually taken against the total available; it's descriptive, not a claim about capacity. If someone only took 1 slice, their ratio is simply 1/8, or 12.5%, regardless of what they could've taken.

Capacity constraints like slots and fleet size explain why some carriers took less—SpiceJet took none and actually lost share, down 34%. Shares always sum to 100%, so Go First's vacated share redistributes fully among the rest, even accounting for market growth; even if some passengers stop flying entirely, the relative shares of others still rise since share is a relative measure, not an absolute count.

Good question. Dividing by 8 **doesn't mean you have to take 8, or any fair share of it.** It only measures **what you actually took**.

### Pizza again
8 slices are left. You're full and can only manage 1.
- You took 1 → 1 ÷ 8 = **12.5%**
- Your friend took 7 → 7 ÷ 8 = **87.5%**

Dividing by 8 didn't force you to eat more. It just records that you took a small part and your friend took most of it.

### Same with airlines
Not every airline *could* take Go First's passengers. To expand, an airline needs:
- **aircraft**, to add flights;
- **slots**, take-off and landing times at busy airports;
- **money**, to lease planes and hire crew.

| Airline | Could it expand? | What it took |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | Yes: big fleet, many slots | **66%** |
| Akasa | Yes: new aircraft arriving | **35%** |
| Air India Group | Yes: new Tata investment | **34%** |
| SpiceJet | **No**: financial trouble, planes grounded | **−34%** (lost share) |

SpiceJet "couldn't take 8", or even 1. So its ratio is low, here even negative. **That's what the ratio is designed to show.** And explaining *why* SpiceJet couldn't take any is exactly where your **slot and fleet evidence** comes in.

### What happens to the slices nobody can eat?
Shares always add up to 100%, so Go First's 8% **always ends up with someone**. If SpiceJet can't take any, the others take more, which is why IndiGo + Akasa + Air India Group together took more than 100%. They also picked up SpiceJet's lost share.

**In one line:** *"The absorption ratio doesn't assume anyone could take the whole exiting share. It measures what each airline actually took, and slot and fleet constraints explain why some took a lot and others took nothing."*

### Pizza again
8 slices are left. You're full and can only manage 1.
- You took 1 → 1 ÷ 8 = **12.5%**
- Your friend took 7 → 7 ÷ 8 = **87.5%**

Dividing by 8 didn't force you to eat more. It just records that you took a small part and your friend took most of it.

### Same with airlines
Not every airline *could* take Go First's passengers. To expand, an airline needs:
- **aircraft**, to add flights;
- **slots**, take-off and landing times at busy airports;
- **money**, to lease planes and hire crew.

| Airline | Could it expand? | What it took |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | Yes: big fleet, many slots | **66%** |
| Akasa | Yes: new aircraft arriving | **35%** |
| Air India Group | Yes: new Tata investment | **34%** |
| SpiceJet | **No**: financial trouble, planes grounded | **−34%** (lost share) |

response.value:
Yes, exactly. One small wording fix on the absorption ratio first: it measures how much the remaining airlines **did** absorb (what actually happened), not how much they **can**.

## Mechanical merger: from separate squares to one square

**Your understanding is right:**
- **Before:** each airline is a separate firm, so each share is squared on its own.
- **After:** they have one owner, so the shares are **added first, then squared**.
- **The formula** just writes the difference in a shorter form.

### Two airlines (simplest case)
Airlines A = 8%, B = 7%.

| | Calculation | HHI contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Before (separate) | 8² + 7² | 64 + 49 = **113** |
| After (one owner) | (8 + 7)² | 15² = **225** |
| **Jump** | 225 − 113 | **112** |

**The shortcut:**
$$(8+7)^2 = 8^2 + 7^2 + \underbrace{2 \times 8 \times 7}_{\text{extra}}$$
The extra part is 2 × 8 × 7 = **112**, the same answer. So:
$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2 \times s_A \times s_B$$

### Three airlines (the real Tata case)
With three airlines, every **pair** adds its own extra part:
$$(a+b+c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + \underbrace{2ab + 2ac + 2bc}_{\text{extra}}$$
That's why the formula has a $\sum$ (sum over all pairs):
$$\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}} = 2\sum_{a<b} s_a s_b$$
($a<b$ just means "count each pair once": AI–Vistara, AI–AirAsia, Vistara–AirAsia.)

**January 2022, shares in December 2021:**

| | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Before (separate) | 8.46² + 7.72² + 6.28² | 71.6 + 59.6 + 39.4 = **170.6** |
| After (one owner) | (8.46 + 7.72 + 6.28)² | 22.46² = **504.4** |
| **Jump (long way)** | 504.4 − 170.6 | **≈ 334** |
| **Jump (formula)** | 2 × (8.46×7.72 + 8.46×6.28 + 7.72×6.28) | 2 × 166.9 = **≈ 334** ✓ |

### Why it's called "mechanical"
It's **pure arithmetic**. It assumes:
- shares are **frozen** at the month before the event;
- **nobody changes behaviour**: no passengers switch, no routes change.

It answers: *"If nothing else happened, how much would HHI rise just from counting these airlines as one?"*

### Why it's useful
Compare it with what **actually** happened:

| Event | Mechanical (expected) | Observed (actual) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2022 | +334 | +373 | **+39** |

- **+334** comes purely from the change of owner.
- **+39** is extra, because the market kept moving (the group grew, others shrank).

**In one line:** *"The mechanical ΔHHI is the jump you get by squaring the combined share instead of squaring each share separately. It shows how much concentration rises from common ownership alone, before anything else changes."*

response.value:
## Contribution to HHI: a simple example

### The basic idea
HHI = the sum of each firm's **share squared**.
So when a firm's share changes, its **square** changes, and that change is its contribution to the change in HHI.

> **Contribution = (share after)² − (share before)²**

That's all $c_g$ is.

### Example: three airlines, one exits

**Before:**
| Airline | Share | Share² |
|---|---|---|
| A | 50 | 2,500 |
| B | 30 | 900 |
| C | 20 | 400 |
| **HHI** | | **3,800** |

**C exits.** Its 20% goes to A (+15) and B (+5).

**After:**
| Airline | Share | Share² |
|---|---|---|
| A | 65 | 4,225 |
| B | 35 | 1,225 |
| **HHI** | | **5,450** |

**HHI rose by 5,450 − 3,800 = +1,650.** Who caused it?

### Step by step: each airline's contribution
| Airline | Before² | After² | Contribution (after² − before²) |
|---|---|---|---|
| C (exits) | 400 | 0 | **−400** |
| A | 2,500 | 4,225 | **+1,725** |
| B | 900 | 1,225 | **+325** |
| **Total** | | | **+1,650** ✓ |

The contributions add up exactly to the total change in HHI. **A caused most of the rise.**

### Why the formula looks like $2s\Delta + \Delta^2$
It's just a shortcut for "after² − before²". With $s$ = share before and $\Delta$ = change:
$$(s+\Delta)^2 - s^2 = 2s\Delta + \Delta^2$$

Check with A: $s = 50$, $\Delta = 15$
$$2 \times 50 \times 15 + 15^2 = 1500 + 225 = 1725 \;✓$$

Check with B: $s = 30$, $\Delta = 5$
$$2 \times 30 \times 5 + 5^2 = 300 + 25 = 325 \;✓$$

### The key insight: the same gain, a different contribution
Suppose A and B **each** gain **+10**:

| Airline | Share before | Gain | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (big) | 50 | +10 | 2×50×10 + 100 = **+1,100** |
| B (small) | 30 | +10 | 2×30×10 + 100 = **+700** |

**The same +10 gain, but A adds far more to concentration**, because the $2s\Delta$ part multiplies the gain by the firm's **existing size**.

> **A gain going to an already big firm raises concentration more than the same gain going to a small firm.**

### Back to the real data (Go First exit)
| Group | Share before | Gain | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| IndiGo (big) | 56.6 | +5.3 | **+631** |
| Air India Group (medium) | 24.6 | +2.7 | +141 |
| Akasa (small) | 1.6 | +2.9 | +18 |

Akasa gained **more** share than the Air India Group (+2.9 vs. +2.7), yet contributed **eight times less** to concentration, because it was small to begin with.

**In one line:** *"Contribution to ΔHHI is each airline's 'after-square minus before-square'. It shows whose gain made the market more concentrated, and gains by already-large firms count much more."*

response.value:
## Contribution to ΔHHI, $c_g$: real data, Go First exit

**The question:** HHI rose after Go First exited. **Which airline groups caused that rise, and by how much?**

### Step 1: Shares before and after (from the decomposition)
| Group | Share before | Share after | Change $\Delta s_g$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 56.56 | 61.89 | +5.33 |
| Air India Group | 24.55 | 27.27 | +2.72 |
| Go First | 8.08 | 0 | −8.08 |
| SpiceJet | 7.64 | 4.91 | −2.72 |
| Akasa Air | 1.64 | 4.50 | +2.86 |
| Others (Alliance, Star, Flybig…) | 1.53 | 1.42 | −0.11 |

### Step 2: The long way, squaring before and after
HHI is the sum of squared shares, so each group's contribution is **(after)² − (before)²**:

| Group | Before² | After² | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 56.56² = 3,199 | 61.89² = 3,831 | **+631** |
| Air India Group | 24.55² = 603 | 27.27² = 744 | **+141** |
| Akasa Air | 1.64² = 3 | 4.50² = 20 | **+18** |
| SpiceJet | 7.64² = 58 | 4.91² = 24 | **−34** |
| Go First | 8.08² = 65 | 0 | **−65** |
| Others | ~1 | ~1 | ~0 |
| **HHI** | **3,930** | **4,620** | **+690** |

### Step 3: The same thing with the formula
$$c_g = 2\,\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}\,\Delta s_g + (\Delta s_g)^2$$

| Group | $2 \times$ before $\times$ change | + change² | $c_g$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 2 × 56.56 × 5.33 = 603 | + 28 | **+631** ✓ |
| Air India Group | 2 × 24.55 × 2.72 = 134 | + 7 | **+141** ✓ |
| Akasa Air | 2 × 1.64 × 2.86 = 9 | + 8 | **+18** ✓ |
| SpiceJet | 2 × 7.64 × (−2.72) = −42 | + 7 | **−34** ✓ |

And for the exiting airline:
$$-\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2 = -(8.08)^2 = -65$$

**Total:**
$$\Delta\text{HHI} = -65 + 631 + 141 + 18 - 34 + 0 \approx \mathbf{+690}$$

The formula gives exactly the same answer as squaring before and after. It just does it group by group.

### Step 4: Read the result
| Group | Contribution | Share of the +690 rise |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | +631 | **≈ 91%** |
| Air India Group | +141 | ≈ 20% |
| Akasa Air | +18 | ≈ 3% |
| SpiceJet | −34 | −5% (shrinking *reduced* concentration) |
| Go First leaving | −65 | −9% (its own square disappears) |

**Three takeaways:**
1. **IndiGo alone caused about 91%** of the rise in concentration. This is what H4b tests ("more than half"). It's a result for Assignment 3.
2. **Akasa vs. Air India Group:** Akasa gained a *bit more* share (+2.86 vs. +2.72) but contributed **8× less** (18 vs. 141). The difference comes from the $2 \times \text{before}$ part: Air India Group started at 24.6%, Akasa at 1.6%.
3. **Negative contributions reduce concentration.** A firm shrinking lowers its square, and the exiting firm's square disappears completely.

### Jet exit, for comparison
| Group | Contribution |
|---|---|
| IndiGo | **+473** |
| SpiceJet | +89 |
| Go First | +39 |
| Vistara + AirAsia India | +37 |
| Air India Group | −3 |
| Jet leaving | −191 |
| **ΔHHI** | **≈ +444** |

Here IndiGo's +473 is **more than the whole +444**. That's possible because the negative parts (Jet's −191) pull the total down. So IndiGo's gain alone raised concentration by more than the market's net rise.

**In one line:** *"$c_g$ splits the change in HHI into one piece per airline group: after-squared minus before-squared. After Go First exited, IndiGo's piece was about 91% of the total rise."*

response.value:
Fair question. "Caused" was a poor word choice. Here's what it really means.

### Go First leaving doesn't directly raise concentration
When Go First stops flying, its passengers still need to fly, so they move to other airlines. **Whether concentration goes up a lot or a little depends on *where* they go.**

### Three "what if" cases
Go First had **8.1%**. Imagine three ways that 8.1% could be shared out:

| Case | Where Go First's 8.1% goes | Change in HHI |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | All to **Akasa** (small, 1.6% → 9.7%) | **+26** (barely changes) |
| **B** | All to **IndiGo** (big, 56.6% → 64.6%) | **+914** (big jump) |
| **What actually happened** | Mostly to IndiGo, some to Air India Group and Akasa | **+690** |

**The same exit, but very different results.** If passengers had gone to a small airline, the market would have stayed about as concentrated as before. Because most went to the **biggest** airline, the market became much more concentrated.

### So what does "91%" mean?
The total rise was **+690**. When you split that rise by airline:
- **+631** came from **IndiGo getting bigger**
- the rest came from the others: Air India Group +141, Akasa +18, SpiceJet −34, Go First disappearing −65

631 ÷ 690 ≈ **91%**.

**In plain words:** *"Of the increase in concentration after Go First left, about 91% is explained by IndiGo's share growing."*

### Why IndiGo's gain counts so much
HHI **squares** shares, so growth by a big firm counts far more:
- IndiGo going from 56.6 to 61.9 → its square rises by **631**.
- Akasa going from 1.6 to 4.5 → its square rises by only **18**.

Both gained roughly 3–5 points of share, but IndiGo was already huge, so its gain moved concentration much more.

### The chain, step by step
```
Go First exits
   → its passengers need another airline
      → most go to IndiGo (it has the planes and slots)
         → IndiGo's share rises 56.6% → 61.9%
            → IndiGo was already big, so HHI jumps
               → ~91% of the HHI rise comes from IndiGo's growth
```

**Better wording for the paper:** use **"accounts for"** instead of "caused", e.g. *"IndiGo's gain accounts for about 91% of the rise in HHI after Go First's exit."*

response.value:
Yes, mostly right. One correction: the observed change doesn't **always** go up, and that's what makes it worth measuring.

## What "consolidation ΔHHI" is
> **The *actual* change in HHI around each Tata step:** average HHI in the 12 months after minus the 12 months before.

It's measured at both levels, brand and ownership, because each Tata step changes a different one.

## Each step, with the real numbers
| Tata step | What changed | Brand HHI (before → after) | Ownership HHI (before → after) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Jan 2022**: Tata takes over Air India | **Owners** 3 → 1 (brands unchanged) | 3,513 → 3,503 = **−10** | 3,513 → 3,886 = **+373** |
| **Dec 2024**: Vistara and AIX Connect merge | **Brands** 4 → 2 (owner unchanged) | 4,066 → 4,559 = **+493** | 4,619 → 4,902 = **+283** |

**How to read it:**
- **January 2022:** only the *owner* changed, so **ownership HHI** jumps (+373). Brand HHI barely moves (−10), because the brands stayed separate.
- **December 2024:** only the *brands* changed, so **brand HHI** jumps (+493). Ownership HHI was already counting them as one group, yet it still rose +283. **That rise isn't from the merger.** It's the market itself moving, as IndiGo kept growing and SpiceJet kept shrinking.

## "Will it obviously increase every time?"
- **The mechanical part, yes.** $2 s_a s_b$ is always positive, so combining firms always adds to HHI on paper.
- **The observed change, not necessarily.** Over 12 months other things happen too: airlines grow or shrink, and demand recovers after COVID. Those can push HHI up or down on top of the merger.

That's exactly why you **compare the two**:

| Step | Mechanical (expected from merger) | Observed (actual) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2022 (ownership) | +334 | +373 | **+39**: a bit more than the merger alone |
| Dec 2024 (brand) | +256 | +493 | **+237**: much more than the merger alone |

**Reading:**
- In **2022**, almost all of the rise is the change of owner.
- In **2024**, only about half is the brand merger. The rest is the market continuing to concentrate.

## A caveat to remember
The January 2022 windows (all of 2021 vs. all of 2022) overlap the **COVID recovery**, so part of the difference may come from demand bouncing back. The analysis notes this in

: *"Confounded by pandemic recovery…"*.

**In one line:** *"Consolidation ΔHHI is the actual change in HHI around each Tata step. We compare it with the mechanical ΔHHI to separate the rise caused by the merger itself from the rise caused by the market moving at the same time."*

response.generatedTitle: Computed passenger and capacity shares using June 2023 data

response.value:
Close, but one important correction: **Q is passengers *or* seat-km. You never divide one by the other.** The calculation is done **twice, separately**:

| Version | Q = | Share = | What it measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Passenger share** | passengers | group's passengers ÷ **all passengers** × 100 | Who **carried** the travellers |
| **Capacity share** | seat-km | group's seat-km ÷ **all seat-km** × 100 | Who **offered** the seats |

Passengers ÷ seats would be the **load factor** (how full the planes are), which is a different thing.

### The formula, symbol by symbol
$$s_{gt} = \frac{Q_{gt}}{\sum_j Q_{jt}} \times 100$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $g$ | the ownership group | IndiGo |
| $t$ | the month | June 2023 |
| $Q_{gt}$ | that group's passengers (or seat-km) that month | IndiGo's passengers in June 2023 |
| $\sum_j Q_{jt}$ | add up $Q$ for **every** group $j$ that month, i.e. the market total | all passengers in June 2023 |
| $s_{gt}$ | the share, in % | IndiGo's share in June 2023 |

### Example 1: Passenger share, June 2023 ($Q$ = passengers)
| Group | Passengers | ÷ total (12,486,601) × 100 |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 7,893,296 | **63.2%** |
| Air India Group | 3,227,764 | **25.9%** |
| Akasa Air | 618,053 | **4.9%** |
| SpiceJet | 555,248 | **4.4%** |

### Example 2: Capacity share, June 2023 ($Q$ = seat-km, in thousands)
| Group | Seat-km | ÷ total (13,309,593) × 100 |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | 8,254,272 | **62.0%** |
| Air India Group | 3,706,151 | **27.8%** |
| Akasa Air | 646,246 | **4.9%** |
| SpiceJet | 583,707 | **4.4%** |

### Why do both?
- **Passenger share:** IndiGo carried **63.2%** of travellers.
- **Capacity share:** IndiGo offered **62.0%** of seats.

These usually match closely, but when they **differ** it tells you something. For example, the Air India Group offered 27.8% of the capacity but carried only 25.9% of the passengers, so its planes were less full than IndiGo's. Around an exit, this comparison is what lets you say whether an airline grew by **adding planes** or by **filling existing seats**.

**In one line:** *"$s_{gt}$ is a group's share of the market in one month. We calculate it twice: once with passengers (who carried the travellers) and once with seat-km (who offered the capacity)."*

Next: $\bar s_g^{\,k}$, the average of these monthly shares over the before and after windows.

response.value:
Yes, with one small fix. For seat-km, divide by the **total seat-km of all groups**, the whole market, not "total seats in that ownership group". Same as for passengers:

- passenger share = group's passengers ÷ **all** passengers × 100
- capacity share = group's seat-km ÷ **all** seat-km × 100

And $\bar s_g^{\,k}$ is the **mean share**, not mean concentration. You've got the idea right.

## What is $W^k$?
$$\bar s_g^{\,k} = \frac{1}{|W^{k}|}\sum_{t \in W^{k}} s_{gt}$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Go First example |
|---|---|---|
| $k$ | which window: "pre" (before) or "post" (after) | pre or post |
| $W^{k}$ | the **list of months** in that window | $W^{\text{pre}}$ = May 2022 … Apr 2023 |
| $\lvert W^{k} \rvert$ | the **number of months** in the list | 12 |
| $t \in W^{k}$ | "for every month $t$ in that list" | May 2022, Jun 2022, … |
| $\sum_{t \in W^{k}} s_{gt}$ | add up the group's monthly shares over those months | sum of IndiGo's 12 shares |
| $\bar s_g^{\,k}$ | that sum ÷ number of months, i.e. the **average** | IndiGo's average before |

**$W$ stands for "window"**: a set of months.

## The windows
| Exit | $W^{\text{pre}}$ (before) | $\lvert W^{\text{pre}}\rvert$ | $W^{\text{post}}$ (after) | $\lvert W^{\text{post}}\rvert$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go First | May 2022 – Apr 2023 | **12** | Jun 2023 – May 2024 | **12** |
| Jet Airways | Apr 2018 – Mar 2019 | **12** | May 2019 – Feb 2020 | **10** (stopped before COVID) |

That's why the method says "**up to** 12 months": Jet's after window is only 10.

**$W^{\text{pre}}$ = May 2022 – Apr 2023:**
| Month | $s_{gt}$ |
|---|---|
| May 22 | 55.59 |
| Jun 22 | 56.90 |
| Jul 22 | 58.85 |
| Aug 22 | 57.65 |
| Sep 22 | 57.72 |
| Oct 22 | 56.76 |

| Dec 22 | 54.94 |
| Jan 23 | 54.56 |

response.value:
Your summary is right, with one small correction: $a_g$ is the portion taken by **each** group $g$, one number per group. All the groups' portions **together** add up to 100%.

Now the sentence you asked about:

> *"A higher $a_g$ for seat-km than for passengers marks capacity-led growth, checked against company filings."*

## Step 1: You calculate $a_g$ twice
Remember $Q$ can be passengers or seat-km. So each group gets **two** absorption ratios:
- **$a_g$ (passengers):** what portion of the exiting airline's **travellers** did this group take?
- **$a_g$ (seat-km):** what portion of the exiting airline's **capacity** (seats offered) did this group take?

## Step 2: Compare the two
| If… | It means… | Called |
|---|---|---|
| seat-km $a_g$ **>** passengers $a_g$ | The group **added seats faster** than it added passengers, i.e. it brought in new planes and flights | **Capacity-led growth** |
| passengers $a_g$ **>** seat-km $a_g$ | The group **filled its existing seats** more, i.e. its planes got fuller | **Demand-led growth** |

### A restaurant example
A big restaurant next door closes, and its customers come to your street.
- **Restaurant A** adds 10 new tables to serve them → it grew its **capacity**.
- **Restaurant B** adds no tables but its empty tables now fill up → it grew through **demand**.

## Step 3: Real example, Jet Airways exit (2019)
| Group | $a_g$ passengers | $a_g$ seat-km | Which is higher? | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SpiceJet** | 22.9% | **30.4%** | seat-km | **Capacity-led**: added planes and flights |
| **IndiGo** | **37.7%** | 28.5% | passengers | **Demand-led**: filled its existing seats |

**SpiceJet** took about 30% of Jet's **seats** but only about 23% of its **passengers**. So it expanded its fleet quickly, a bit faster than it could fill those new seats.

## Step 4: "Checked against company filings"
If the data says SpiceJet grew by adding capacity, you look for **proof** in its own documents. **SpiceJet's Annual Report 2019–20 (p. 62)** says that after a full-service carrier (Jet) stopped flying:
- SpiceJet was **allotted 74 slots** (take-off and landing times at busy airports)
- SpiceJet **inducted 31 aircraft** (added planes to its fleet)

**The data and the filing agree:** the data shows capacity-led growth, and the filing says *how* (Jet's slots and planes). That's what "checked against company filings" means.

## The whole Stage 2 in one picture
```
Δs_g  = after − before                → how much each group's share changed
a_g   = Δs_g ÷ exiting share × 100     → what portion of the exit each group took
            ├─ using passengers         → who took the travellers
            └─ using seat-km            → who took the capacity
Compare the two:
   seat-km higher  → added planes/flights → check filings for slots & aircraft
   passengers higher → filled existing seats
```

**In one line:** *"We calculate the absorption ratio with both passengers and seat-km. If seat-km is higher, the airline grew by adding planes and flights, and we check that against its own filings, e.g. SpiceJet's 74 slots and 31 aircraft after Jet's exit."*

Remember $Q$ can be passengers or seat-km. So each group gets **two** absorption ratios:
- **$a_g$ (passengers):** what portion of the exiting airline's **travellers** did this group take?
- **$a_g$ (seat-km):** what portion of the exiting airline's **capacity** (seats offered) did this group take?

## Step 2: Compare the two
| If… | It means… | Called |
|---|---|---|
| seat-km $a_g$ **>** passengers $a_g$ | The group **added seats faster** than it added passengers, i.e. it brought in new planes and flights | **Capacity-led growth** |
| passengers $a_g$ **>** seat-km $a_g$ | The group **filled its existing seats** more, i.e. its planes got fuller | **Demand-led growth** |

### A restaurant example
A big restaurant next door closes, and its customers come to your street.
- **Restaurant A** adds 10 new tables to serve them → it grew its **capacity**.
- **Restaurant B** adds no tables but its empty tables now fill up → it grew through **demand**.

response.value:
Yes, the overall idea is right: **after an exit, which group's gain raised concentration the most?** Two corrections to the formula, though.

### Correction 1: in $c_g$, use the group's **own** share before, not the exiting airline's
$$c_g = 2 \times \underbrace{\bar s_g^{\,\text{pre}}}_{\text{group } g\text{'s own share before}} \times \underbrace{\Delta s_g}_{\text{group } g\text{'s change}} + (\Delta s_g)^2$$

| Group | Its own share before | Its change | $c_g$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | **56.56** | +5.33 | 2 × 56.56 × 5.33 + 5.33² = **+631** |
| Akasa | **1.64** | +2.86 | 2 × 1.64 × 2.86 + 2.86² = **+18** |

That's the whole point: IndiGo's **own** large starting share is what makes its contribution so big.

### Correction 2: $\Delta\text{HHI}$ adds up **contributions**, not "concentration"
$$\Delta\text{HHI} = \underbrace{-\big(\bar s_x^{\,\text{pre}}\big)^2}_{\text{exiting airline's square disappears}} + \underbrace{\sum_{g\neq x} c_g}_{\text{add up every other group's contribution}}$$

Go First example:
$$\Delta\text{HHI} = -(8.08)^2 + (631 + 141 + 18 - 34 + \ldots) = -65 + 755 \approx \mathbf{+690}$$

### The two parts in order
| Step | What you calculate | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| 1. $c_g$ for each group | after² − before² for that group | "How much did **this group** change HHI?" |
| 2. $\Delta\text{HHI}$ | exiting airline's −square + all the $c_g$ added up | "How much did **total** HHI change?" |
| 3. Compare | $c_g$ ÷ $\Delta\text{HHI}$ | "What **portion** of the rise came from each group?" (IndiGo ≈ 91%) |

**In one line:** *"$c_g$ is each group's own contribution to the change in HHI, based on its own starting share and its change. Adding all of them, minus the exiting airline's square, gives the total change in HHI. That shows whose gain drove concentration up."*

response.value:
Your summary is right. One small fix: **before** = sum of the squares (each brand squared separately), **after** = square of the sum (shares added first, then squared). The difference is the mechanical change.

Now the line you asked about: **"for brands $G$ at shares in the month before the event"**. It has two parts.

### Part 1: "for brands $G$"
$G$ is just a name for **the group of brands that come under one owner** at that step.

| Step | Brands in $G$ |
|---|---|
| January 2022 | Air India (+ AI Express), Vistara, AirAsia India |
| December 2024 | Air India + Vistara; Air India Express + AIX Connect |

Only these brands go into the formula. IndiGo, SpiceJet and the others aren't part of the merger, so they're left out.

### Part 2: "at shares in the month before the event"
To calculate $2 \times s_a \times s_b$, you need actual numbers for $s_a$, $s_b$, … The question is **which month's shares to use**.

**Answer:** the last normal month **just before** the step.

| Step | Shares taken from | Shares used |
|---|---|---|
| January 2022 | **December 2021** | Air India 8.46, Vistara 7.72, AirAsia India 6.28 |
| December 2024 | **September 2024** (October–November are the half-merged months) | Air India 11.14, Vistara 10.04, AI Express 3.97, AIX Connect 4.11 |

### Why the month before?
Because you want the jump from the **ownership change alone**, before anything else moves.
- If you used shares from a later month, they'd already include the airlines growing or shrinking after the merger.
- Freezing the shares at the month before isolates the pure effect of "these brands now count as one".

That's what makes it **mechanical**: same shares, only the counting changes.

### Plain-English version of the line
> *"We take the brands that come under one owner, use their market shares from the month just before the merger, and calculate how much HHI rises just from counting them together."*

response.value:
Yes, that's right. A bit more on each part, so you can defend it if asked:

**1. "Too few for a regression"**
A regression needs **many observations** to estimate an effect and test whether it's real or just noise. You have **2 exits and 2 consolidation steps**, so 4 events in total. With 4 data points you can't separate the effect of the exit from everything else going on, or say whether a result is statistically significant. The issue isn't prediction; it's that **there isn't enough data to estimate reliably**.

(O1 already uses a regression across all 138 months. Your O2 doesn't repeat that. It goes deeper into each event.)

**2. "Decomposition shows directly where the share went"**
The decomposition is **exact accounting**: the changes add up to the exiting airline's share (absorption sums to 100%), and the contributions add up to the change in HHI. Nothing is estimated or assumed. It shows directly **who gained and by how much**, which is exactly what O2 asks.

**3. "The filings explain why"**
The numbers show **what** happened. The company filings (SpiceJet's 74 slots and 31 aircraft, Go First's grounded engines) show **how and why**: the slot and fleet evidence.

**4. "The CCI order grounds the policy discussion"**
The CCI order is the regulator's **own written reasoning**, so the competition-policy discussion rests on what CCI actually said, not on news reports. That's what feedback #6 asked for.

**If someone asks "why not a regression?":**
> *"With only two exits and two consolidation steps, a regression can't produce reliable estimates. Instead we use an exact before-and-after decomposition that shows where each exiting share went, and we explain the mechanism using company filings and the CCI order."*

Let's drop the formulas and use a simple story.

### A story with three friends' money
Three friends each have some money **yesterday**:
- Asha: ₹8
- Bina: ₹7
- Chitra: ₹6

**Today they decide to put it all in one shared wallet.**

**Question 1: How much is in the shared wallet *because* they combined?**
Just add yesterday's amounts: 8 + 7 + 6 = **₹21**.
You didn't wait to see anything. You used **yesterday's real numbers** and simply **counted them together**.
→ This is the **mechanical** number.

**Question 2: How much is *actually* in the wallet a year later?**
You look at the wallet over the next year. It's **₹25**: they earned a bit more after combining.
→ This is the **observed** number.

**Comparing them:**
- ₹21 came from **combining** alone.
- The extra ₹4 came from **what happened afterwards**, not from combining.

### Now the same with Tata
| | Friends | Tata |
|---|---|---|
| Separate before | Asha, Bina, Chitra | Air India, Vistara, AirAsia India |
| Real numbers the day before | ₹8, ₹7, ₹6 | 8.46%, 7.72%, 6.28% (December 2021) |
| **Mechanical**: just count them as one | ₹21 | HHI **+334** |
| **Observed**: what really happened over the next year | ₹25 | HHI **+373** |
| Extra from later changes | ₹4 | **+39** |

- **Mechanical** = take the **real** shares from the month before, and **just count the airlines as one**. No waiting, no guessing. It answers: *"How much does concentration rise **only because** they now have one owner?"*
- **Observed** = look at what **actually** happened over the next 12 months.
- **The difference** = how much changed **for other reasons** (airlines growing or shrinking).

(For HHI the combining step uses squares instead of simple adding, as we did before, but the idea is the same.)

## Testable hypotheses for O2

A testable hypothesis is a clear statement of **what you expect to find**, written so that the data can later show it as **supported or rejected**. In Assignment 3 you'll check each one.

You have three: **H4a and H4b** for the exits (Part A), and **H4c** for the consolidation (Part B).

### H4a: Exit absorption
> *We expect IndiGo's absorption ratio to be the largest of any group after both exits, and larger after Go First than after Jet Airways.*

| | |
|---|---|
| **Uses** | $a_g$ (Stage 2) |
| **Why we expect it** | IndiGo had the most aircraft and slots, so it was best placed to take over the exiting airlines' passengers. By 2023 its rivals were weaker (SpiceJet struggling), so it should take an even bigger portion. |
| **Supported if** | (1) IndiGo's $a_g$ is the highest of all groups after Jet **and** after Go First, **and** (2) its $a_g$ after Go First > its $a_g$ after Jet |
| **Rejected if** | Any other group took a bigger portion, or IndiGo's portion was smaller after Go First |
| **Early check** | IndiGo 38% (Jet) → 66% (Go First), the largest both times, so it looks **supported** (confirm in Assignment 3) |

### H4b: Exit-driven concentration
> *We expect IndiGo's gain to account for more than half of the rise in HHI after each exit.*

| | |
|---|---|
| **Uses** | $c_g$ and $\Delta\text{HHI}$ (Stage 3) |
| **Why we expect it** | HHI squares shares, so a gain by the biggest firm raises concentration the most. |
| **Supported if** | $c_{\text{IndiGo}} \div \Delta\text{HHI} > 50\%$ after **both** exits |
| **Rejected if** | IndiGo accounts for 50% or less after either exit |
| **Early check** | Jet: 473 ÷ 444 > 100%. Go First: 631 ÷ 690 ≈ 91%. Looks **supported** |

### H4c: Tata consolidation
> *We expect the observed rise in HHI at each Tata step to be at least the mechanical rise from common ownership alone.*

| | |
|---|---|
| **Uses** | $\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}}$ vs. the observed ΔHHI (Part B) |
| **Why we expect it** | After a merger, the combined group usually keeps growing while rivals weaken, so the actual rise should be **at least** what ownership alone explains. |
| **Supported if** | Observed ≥ mechanical at **both** steps |
| **Rejected if** | Observed < mechanical at either step, meaning rivals gained ground and partly offset the merger |
| **Early check** | January 2022: 373 ≥ 334 ✓. December 2024: 493 ≥ 256 ✓. Looks **supported** |

### How they fit together
```
Part A (Exits)
   H4a → WHO took the most share?             (absorption ratio)
   H4b → WHOSE gain raised concentration most? (contribution to ΔHHI)

Part B (Consolidation)
   H4c → Did HHI rise at least as much as ownership alone explains?
         (observed vs mechanical)
```

**Two things to keep in mind:**
1. The "early checks" are only so you understand the hypotheses. **They don't go in Assignment 2.** You report them in Assignment 3.
2. A hypothesis can be **rejected** and still score well, as long as you explain why. The guidelines reward honest, well-argued results.

**In one line:** *"H4a tests who absorbed the most, H4b tests whose gain drove concentration, and H4c tests whether the Tata mergers raised concentration at least as much as common ownership alone would."*

Next: **anticipated challenges**.

## How the cleanup is validated

Permalink: How the cleanup is validated
DGCA's workbooks are genuinely messy (a `PASSENEGER` header typo, shifting S3 keys, 2-digit years, the same airport under several
spellings). Every cleanup decision is checkable and re-run on every refresh, because a naive heuristic would silently corrupt the data:


• Goa is two airports. Dabolim (`GOI`) and Mopa (`GOX`, opened 2023) - and DGCA files Mopa's traffic under Dabolim's IATA code. Merging them erases an airport; trusting the code mislabels one.
Resolved by cited research, encoded with validity windows.
• The overlap gate refuses to sum two concurrent source labels into one airport unless a human has
declared it - a new DGCA label landing on an existing airport reds CI until
classified, never silently merges.
...

## How the cleanup is validated
...

test. `validate --assumptions` re-tests each against current data → HOLDS/TRIGGERED/STALE/ORPHANED in [DATA_QUALITY.md](https://github.com/mkubicek/india-aviation-stats/blob/main/data/processed/DATA_QUALITY.md).

I'm also confirming the mechanical merger HHI formula renders correctly and noting that Section 5.4's O4 objective still needs its "compare brand" language addressed.

More substantive issues: there's team inconsistency since the objective originally tied to O4 now seems to sit under O1 instead, and H3 also appears under O4 — both need flagging. Most pressing though is that the main body spans roughly 6.5 pages against a stated 2–3 page limit, which is a strong violation I need to call out. I read the whole PDF. **Your O2 parts are consistent and make sense from start to finish.** I found three small wording fixes in your sections, and some bigger issues in the rest of the paper that the team needs to sort out.

## Your O2 thread, end to end

| Section | What it says | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Objective O2** | Exits (Jet 2019, Go First 2023), slot and fleet evidence, the Tata rise from common ownership, CCI for the policy discussion | ✅ |
| **2. Unit table** | Ownership group before vs. after each exit; market-month before vs. after each Tata step | ✅ Matches the method |
| **3. Data sources** | Company filings (#5) and CCI order (#6), both used for O2, with bulleted limitations | ✅ |
| **4. Variables** | $\Delta s_g$, $a_g$, $c_g$, $\Delta\text{HHI}^{\text{mech}}$, consolidation ΔHHI | ✅ Every formula in §5.2 has a matching variable |
| **5.2 Method** | Exits Stages 1–3, Consolidation Stage 1, Justification | ✅ No results stated, method only |
| **6.1 Hypotheses** | H4a (absorption), H4b (concentration), H4c (Tata) | ✅ Each one maps to a stage |
| **6.2 Challenges** | Confounding trends, small sample, reverse causality, market definitions | ✅ |
| **Appendix A** | `carrier_monthly.csv` plus dictionary | ✅ |
| **Appendix B** | Missing mechanism documents | ✅ |

**Three small wording fixes I'd make in your parts:**
1. **Variables table, $c_g$ row:** says "part of the post-exit rise in HHI **caused by** group g". We agreed "accounts for" is safer, so it should read **"accounted for by group g"**.
2. **Challenge "Confounding trends":** "**Addressed** with 6-month windows…" sounds like it's already done. Better: "**Checked in Assignment 3** with 6-month windows…".
3. **Appendix A source note:** "at the commit recorded in **Section 3**", but Section 3 doesn't show the commit; the reference list does. Better: "at the commit cited in the references".

## General issues (team-wide)

**Important:**
1. **Page limit.** Sections 1–6 run from page 1 to page 7, about **6.5 pages**, against a **2–3 page** limit. This is the biggest risk. The gray sections will need heavy trimming once they're written.
2. **Submission date** on the cover says **October 18, 2026**, and today is October 20. Check whether the deadline moved and update the date.
3. **O1 vs. O4 overlap.** The new O1 objective covers brand vs. ownership vs. modified HHI (F1). But **§5.4 (O4 method)** and **H3** still list that comparison under O4. The owners of O1 and O4 should agree on where it belongs.
4. **O4 objective vs. O4 method.** The objective promises route-level checks and a resilience measure, but **§5.4 only describes the duopoly cut-offs**. The method for routes and spare capacity is missing.
5. **Route data.** The O4 unit row and the Section 3 row "DGCA city-pair traffic [availability to check]" are still open. As found earlier, the GitHub route file has **no airline breakdown**, so it can't produce route HHI.

**Placeholders still in gray:** the Section 1 "what changed" sentence, MHHI formula and stakes, duopoly cut-offs [x], the O3 entrant list, the O1 and O3 justifications, H6 threshold, Appendix B intro, and Appendix C (AI disclosure).

**Layout (easy fixes):**
- The **"2. Unit of Analysis"** heading sits alone at the bottom of page 1.
- The **Table 2 caption** is on page 2, but the table itself starts on page 3.
- The **"5. Methodology"** heading sits alone at the bottom of page 4.

These will probably shift once the team trims, so it's best to fix them last.

**Minor:** the title says "between 2015–2026". It should be "between 2015 and 2026" or "2015–2026" without "between".

Should I make the three fixes in your parts now?

I'm breaking down O1's three-tier concentration analysis: brand vs. ownership vs. modified HHI, plus CR2, effective firm count, and IndiGo's dominance via market power ratio. The unit is market-month, but I'm noting a potential inconsistency—the data source is Kubicek's carrier_monthly rather than DGCA's brand-level "Market Share (%)" field directly, which mixes sources. I'm working through concrete examples like the June 2023 brand-vs-ownership gap (4,266 vs 4,710, a 444-point grouping effect) and how MHHI incorporates partial stakes like SIA's 25.1% in Air India. I'm also explaining the segmented regression intuition—trend plus jumps at four events plus COVID and month dummies, with Newey-West standard errors—and computing IndiGo's market power ratio (63.2/25.9 = 2.44), while questioning whether the "market power index" as HHI/100 is just a rescaling without real substance. Now I'm starting to list the issues worth flagging for critique.

Flagging several problems: the "market power" terminology conflicts with F7's instruction to restrict claims to structural measures—terms like "unilateral market power," "dominance flag," and "market power index" should probably be renamed to something like "relative dominance ratio" since the paper itself admits the ratio doesn't directly measure pricing influence. I'm also noting that the HHI/10000×100 rescaling adds no real information under a misleading name, and that the MHHI section mixes two different formulations (O'Brien–Salop vs. Azar) with inconsistent notation—reusing β for both ownership weight and financial interest, inconsistent "Control-HHI" vs. "Ownership-HHI" terminology, and an unsourced claim that β ∈ [0.025, 0.05] comes from SEBI disclosures. The SIA 25.1% stake claim about enforcing "mutual forbearance" also strikes me as an overstated assertion needing scrutiny.

More significantly, I'm realizing SIA's stake is within the Air India Group, not a cross-holding between rival airlines, so it shouldn't drive MHHI unless SIA holds interest in a competitor—and since Air India is privately held by Tata (unlisted) while IndiGo and SpiceJet are listed, institutional cross-ownership between IndiGo and Air India Group is essentially nonexistent. This is a real conceptual flaw I should explain carefully, along with the mismatched data-source claim that DGCA traffic reports contain ownership stakes, which they don't. response.value:
## What MHHI is, in plain words

**Normal HHI assumes rivals are completely separate.** But sometimes an owner of one airline **also owns part of a rival**. Then that owner gains when the rival does well, so the first airline has less reason to compete hard against it.

**MHHI (Modified HHI)** adds an extra term to HHI for these overlapping interests:
$$\text{MHHI} = \text{HHI} + \sum_{j}\sum_{k\neq j} w_{jk}\, s_j\, s_k$$
- $s_j$, $s_k$ are the shares of rival firms $j$ and $k$
- $w_{jk}$ is **how much firm $j$ cares about firm $k$'s profit** (0 = not at all, 1 = as much as its own)

The idea comes from O'Brien & Salop (2000).

### A simple example
| Firm | Share |
|---|---|
| A | 40 |
| B | 30 |
| C | 30 |

HHI = 40² + 30² + 30² = **3,400**

Now A's owner buys **20% of B** as a passive stake, with no control. A now partly cares about B's profit: $w_{AB} = 0.2$.
$$\text{MHHI} = 3{,}400 + 0.2 \times 40 \times 30 = 3{,}400 + 240 = \mathbf{3{,}640}$$

The extra **240** is the "partial-ownership effect": concentration that normal HHI misses.

### Two ways this overlap can happen
| Type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Cross-ownership** | One company owns part of a rival, directly or through a shared parent | Tata owning parts of both Vistara and AirAsia India |
| **Common ownership** | The same **investors** (mutual funds, insurers) own shares in several rivals | Azar et al. (2018): the same big funds own every major US airline |

## Is it applicable to our paper?

### Common ownership (what `o1.tex` uses): ❌ mostly not
`o1.tex` builds MHHI on **mutual funds owning shares in rival airlines** (Azar et al.). That doesn't fit India:

| Airline | Stock-listed? | Can mutual funds hold it? |
|---|---|---|
| IndiGo | ✅ Yes | ✅ |
| SpiceJet | ✅ Yes | ✅ |
| **Air India Group** | ❌ **No** (owned by Tata and SIA) | ❌ |
| Akasa | ❌ No (private) | ❌ |

- The two **biggest** players, IndiGo and the Air India Group, **can't** share fund owners, because Air India isn't on the stock market.
- The only possible overlap is **IndiGo–SpiceJet**, and SpiceJet is about 4%. Rough size: with small fund stakes, the extra term is about **20–30 points** on an HHI of about 5,000. That's negligible.
- **SIA's 25.1% is inside the Air India Group.** SIA owns no rival Indian airline, so it adds **no** cross-ownership with IndiGo. The "mutual forbearance" argument isn't supported.

### Cross-ownership through Tata, before 2022: ✅ this is where MHHI *does* apply
Before January 2022, the paper treats **Vistara** and **AirAsia India** as **separate groups**. But **Tata owned part of both**:
